The segments in Section 8 were built from purchase behaviour only. Demographics were deliberately left out of the clustering, so that the groups describe how households buy rather than who they are. This section brings the demographics back to answer the client’s next question: who are the households in each segment, and how can they be reached?

9.1 Which three demographics, and why

Each variable was chosen because a difference between segments on it leads to a different business action (Table 27).

# The three demographics used to profile the segments
profile_vars <- c("SEC", "HS", "AGE")

# Missing values per profile variable (zeros were turned into NA in Section 7)
profile_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(all_of(profile_vars), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

tibble(
  variable = profile_vars,
  type     = c("Ordinal, 1 high to 4 low", "Numeric, number of members",
               "Ordinal, 1 young to 4 old"),
  action   = c("Price point and value or premium range",
               "Pack size and multi-packs",
               "Media channel and message")
) |>
  left_join(profile_missing, by = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", type = "Type",
             action = "Business lever it informs",
             n_missing = "Missing households")
other_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(c(FEH, MT, SEX, EDU, CHILD, CS, Affluence),
                   \(x) sum(is.na(x))))
share_female <- mean(soap_clean$SEX == 2, na.rm = TRUE)
# Spearman correlation, because SEC is ordinal
sec_aff_cor  <- cor(soap_clean$SEC, soap_clean$Affluence, method = "spearman",
                    use = "complete.obs")
  • SEC (socioeconomic class) tells a manufacturer what price a segment can bear. SEC is also one of the strata the panel was sampled on, so all 600 households have a value and each class holds exactly a quarter of the panel, which makes any tilt within a segment easy to read.
  • HS (household size) is the demographic most directly tied to how much soap a household uses, so it tells the client which segments suit larger packs or multi-packs. 68 households have no size recorded and are left out of the HS summaries only.
  • AGE (age of the homemaker) tells an advertising agency where and how to speak to each segment. Every household has a value.

Why not the others. Affluence overlaps with SEC (Spearman correlation -0.61; SEC runs from 1 high to 4 low, so a negative value means wealthier households sit in the higher classes) and has 68 missing households. MT (native language) and CHILD are codes with no labels in the data guide, so a difference could not be turned into an action. SEX barely varies: 96% of homemakers with a recorded value are female. EDU, FEH and CS are missing for 73, 69 and 99 households and are less directly linked to a bath soap decision. Section 9.5 tests this choice against the data.

Missing values. No household is dropped from the segmentation. For HS, each summary and test uses only the households that have a value, and the number used is shown.

9.2 Profile by group

# Attach the three demographics (and TotalVol, to link size to volume) to each
# household's segment
profile_df <- soap_clusters |>
  select(MemberID, cluster, segment) |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(profile_vars), TotalVol),
            by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(
    # Readable labels for the ordinal codes
    SEC = factor(SEC, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 High", "2", "3", "4 Low")),
    AGE = factor(AGE, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 Young", "2", "3", "4 Old")),
    segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_names)
  )

# One chart function for both categorical variables, so they look the same
plot_props <- function(data, var, title) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ var }})) |>
    count(segment, {{ var }}) |>
    group_by(segment) |>
    mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>                 # share within each segment
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(prop, fct_rev(segment), fill = {{ var }})) +
    geom_col(colour = "white") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
    labs(title = title, y = NULL, x = "Share of households in the segment",
         fill = NULL)
}

# Per-segment summary used in the text and in the summary table
seg_profile <- profile_df |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(households = n(),
            sec_high  = mean(as.integer(SEC) <= 2),     # SEC 1 or 2
            sec_low   = mean(as.integer(SEC) == 4),     # SEC 4
            hs_n      = sum(!is.na(HS)),
            hs_mean   = mean(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            hs_median = median(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            age_old   = mean(AGE == "4 Old"),
            volume    = mean(TotalVol))
# Cramer's V (Cramer, 1946): chi-squared rescaled to run from 0 to 1
cramers_v <- function(tab, stat) sqrt(stat / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1)))

# Chi-squared test plus Cramer's V for one categorical variable
chisq_row <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(d$segment, d[[var]])
  # simulated p-value, see below
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 5000)
  tibble(variable = var, test = "Chi-squared", n = sum(tab),
         p_value = res$p.value,
         effect = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         effect_measure = "Cramer's V")
}

# only households with a recorded size
hs_df <- profile_df |> filter(!is.na(HS))

set.seed(55789)   # the simulated p-values are random, so fix them
kw_hs <- kruskal.test(HS ~ segment, data = hs_df)

profile_tests <- bind_rows(
  chisq_row(profile_df, "SEC"),
  tibble(variable = "HS", test = "Kruskal-Wallis", n = nrow(hs_df),
         p_value = kw_hs$p.value,
         # epsilon squared
         effect = unname(kw_hs$statistic) / (nrow(hs_df) - 1),
         effect_measure = "Epsilon squared"),
  chisq_row(profile_df, "AGE")
)

# Small helpers for the text
seg_prof <- \(seg, col) seg_profile[[col]][seg_profile$segment == seg]
fmt_p    <- \(p) if_else(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste("p =", sprintf("%.3f",
                                                                      p)))
test_row <- \(var) profile_tests |> filter(variable == var)

9.2.1 Socioeconomic class

plot_props(profile_df, SEC, "Socioeconomic class within each segment")

Figure 10 shows the class mix. Because the panel is stratified on SEC, every class holds 25% of households overall, so a segment that departs from a quarter in a class genuinely leans that way. The Loyal promotion buyers have the most lower-class households: 43% are in SEC 4. Together with their high use of other promotions (Section 8), this points to a budget-conscious group that stays with one brand but buys more of it when it is on offer, so price promotions on their favourite brand reach them well. The Promo-6 buyers lean the other way, with 60% in SEC 1 or 2 against 50% overall: their heavy use of promotion 6 looks like a deal-seeking habit rather than a sign that they cannot afford full price, so the timing of promotion 6 matters more than a cheaper product. The test confirms a real but small difference (p = 0.010, Cram<U+00E9>r’s V = 0.131), so SEC is a useful secondary guide, not a targeting rule on its own.

9.2.2 Household size

hs_df |>
  ggplot(aes(HS, fct_rev(segment), fill = segment)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 4, size = 3,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(title = "Household size within each segment",
       subtitle = paste0("Households with a recorded size: n = ", nrow(hs_df)),
       y = NULL, x = "Members in the household")

Figure 11 shows household size. The Heavy multi-brand shoppers have the largest households (5.1 members on average against 4.7 overall) and also buy the most soap, which fits the simple logic that more people use more soap. For a client this is the natural segment for family packs and multi-packs, ideally tied to one brand to counter their habit of spreading volume across brands. The Small-brand regular-price buyers and Promo-6 buyers have the smallest households (4.4 and 4.4 members), so standard packs suit them. The difference is statistically significant but small (p < 0.001, epsilon squared = 0.039).

One pattern needs a warning: only 6 of the 35 Light occasional buyers have a recorded household size. The largest share of the 68 households with no household size (which also lack education, language, gender, TV and Affluence, Section 7) falls into this segment (29 of them), so it may partly reflect households with incomplete panel records rather than a true customer type, so its household size profile should not be relied on. Its SEC and AGE are recorded for every household, so those two comparisons still hold.

9.2.3 Age of the homemaker

plot_props(profile_df, AGE, "Age of the homemaker within each segment")

Figure 12 shows that age does not separate the segments (p = 0.757, Cram<U+00E9>r’s V = 0.078). Older homemakers are the largest group in every segment, from 37% to 55% in the oldest class, and the differences in the chart are within what chance would produce. The practical conclusion is that age gives no reason to reach one segment through a different media channel from another.

9.3 Are the differences real?

A chart can show a difference that is only noise, so each variable is tested. SEC and AGE are categorical, so a chi-squared test of independence checks whether the mix of classes differs between segments. Some cells are small (few households have the youngest age code), so the p-value is simulated rather than taken from the chi-squared table, which keeps it valid when expected counts are below 5. HS is a count with a long right tail, so the Kruskal-Wallis test, which compares segments on ranks rather than means, is used instead of ANOVA. With 600 households even a tiny difference can be “significant”, so an effect size is also reported: Cram<U+00E9>r’s V (Cramér 1946) for the categorical variables and epsilon squared for HS, both running from 0 (no association) to 1.

profile_tests |>
  select(variable, test, n, p_value, effect, effect_measure) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(effect, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(p_value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", test = "Test", n = "Households used",
             p_value = "p-value", effect = "Effect size",
             effect_measure = "Measure")

Table 28 gives the results. SEC and household size differ significantly between segments, but both effects are small, and age does not differ at all. The segments are therefore only weakly visible in demographics. That is a finding in itself, and it supports XYZ’s move to behavioural segmentation: a client could not have found these segments from demographics alone, so targeting should run on purchase data (panel or loyalty card records), with SEC and household size used to fine-tune the offer.

The next two sections go beyond the question. They show which segments and classes cause the differences, and test whether a better demographic was left out.

9.4 Extra check: where do the differences come from?

The tests above say whether the segments differ. This check says which segment and class cause it, so a client knows where to act. For SEC and AGE, the standardised residual of each cell compares the number of households in that segment and class with the number expected if every segment had the same mix. A value beyond <U+00B1>2 marks a clear excess (positive) or shortfall (negative). For HS, pairwise Wilcoxon tests compare every pair of segments, with the Holm adjustment keeping the overall chance of a false difference at 5% across all the comparisons.

# Standardised residuals of the segment by class table, in long form for
# plotting
resid_df <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(segment = d$segment, level = d[[var]])
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning. Only the residuals are used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  as.data.frame.table(res$stdres, responseName = "resid") |>
    mutate(variable = var)
}

plot_resid <- function(rd, title) {
  ggplot(rd, aes(level, fct_rev(segment), fill = resid)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(resid, 1), colour = abs(resid) > 2),
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal_ink, `FALSE` = pal_ink)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal_lo, mid = "white", high = pal_hi,
                         midpoint = 0) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Residual")
}

sec_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "SEC")
age_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "AGE")

plot_resid(sec_resid, "Socioeconomic class") +
  plot_resid(age_resid, "Age of the homemaker")
hs_pairs <- pairwise.wilcox.test(hs_df$HS, hs_df$segment,
                                 p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE) |>
  tidy()

hs_pairs |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(p.value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(group1 = "Segment", group2 = "Compared with",
             p.value = "Holm-adjusted p-value")
resid_text <- \(seg, lvl) {
  sprintf("%+.1f",
          sec_resid$resid[sec_resid$segment == seg & sec_resid$level == lvl])
}
n_age_cells <- sum(abs(age_resid$resid) > 2)

Figure 13 and Table 29 show the detail. The SEC result is driven by three segments: the Loyal promotion buyers have more SEC 4 households than expected (+3.0), the Promo-6 buyers have more SEC 2 households (+2.3), and the small Light occasional group has more SEC 1 households (+2.5). No age cell goes beyond 2 in either direction, which matches the non-significant age test. For household size, only the pairs in the table above differ after adjustment, and every one of them involves the Heavy multi-brand shoppers’ larger households. These are the comparisons a client should rely on when choosing which segment gets which offer.

9.5 Extra check: did we miss a better demographic?

The three variables were chosen for business reasons. As a check, every demographic is measured on how strongly it separates the segments with one common measure, Cram<U+00E9>r’s V. Numeric variables (HS, Affluence and EDU, which has nine sparse levels) are first cut into four equal-sized groups, and native-language codes held by fewer than 20 households are pooled, so that rare codes do not inflate the measure.

all_demo_v <- map_dfr(demo_cols, \(v) {
  d <- soap_clusters |>
    select(MemberID, segment) |>
    left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, value = all_of(v)),
              by = "MemberID") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))
  grp <- if (v %in% c("HS", "Affluence", "EDU")) {
    # numeric: four equal-sized groups
    factor(ntile(d$value, 4))
  } else {
    # categorical: pool rare codes
    fct_lump_min(factor(d$value), min = 20)
  }
  tab <- table(d$segment, grp)
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning. Only the statistic is used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  tibble(variable = v, n = nrow(d),
         cramers_v = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         chosen = v %in% profile_vars)
})

all_demo_v |>
  ggplot(aes(cramers_v, fct_reorder(variable, cramers_v), fill = chosen)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Chosen", `FALSE` = "Not chosen")) +
  labs(title = "How strongly each demographic separates the segments",
       x = "Cramer's V", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
demo_v <- \(v) round(all_demo_v$cramers_v[all_demo_v$variable == v], 3)

Figure 14 shows that every demographic separates the segments only weakly (the largest V is 0.154), which repeats the finding above. HS and SEC are among the stronger variables, which supports two of the three choices. Affluence (V = 0.154) and EDU (0.153) separate the segments more than AGE (0.078). They were left out because Affluence largely repeats SEC and EDU has many sparse levels and more missing values. Since the brief lets the team choose any three demographics, Affluence would be an acceptable alternative to AGE. It is reported here so a reader can see the trade-off rather than take the choice on trust.

9.6 Summary profile of each segment

seg_profile |>
  select(segment, households, sec_high, sec_low, hs_median, hs_mean, age_old) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(c(sec_high, sec_low, age_old), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(hs_mean, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             sec_high = "SEC 1 or 2", sec_low = "SEC 4",
             hs_median = "Median size", hs_mean = "Mean size",
             age_old = "Homemaker AGE 4") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Socioeconomic class", columns = c(sec_high, sec_low)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Household size", columns = c(hs_median, hs_mean))

Table 30 brings the profile together. Putting purchase behaviour (Section 8) and demographics together:

  • Heavy multi-brand shoppers: the largest households and the most volume. Family packs and multi-packs, combined with a reward scheme that concentrates their spending on one brand.
  • Loyal promotion buyers: the most lower-class households (43% in SEC 4). Value packs and price promotions on the brand they already favour.
  • Promo-6 buyers: more higher-class households than average (60% in SEC 1 or 2). Promotion 6 offers spread through the year; a cheaper product is not needed.
  • Loyal regular-price buyers: demographically close to the average household. Reward schemes rather than discounts, which they do not need.
  • Small-brand regular-price buyers: close to average with smaller households, so demographics give little extra help in finding them; they are best reached through purchase data, with trial and visibility to win them from small brands.
  • Light occasional buyers: too small, too light and too poorly recorded (29 of 35 have no household size, education or TV record) to target separately.

10 Question 3: Dimension Reduction with PCA

Question 2 described each household with six purchase behaviour variables. Principal component analysis (PCA) asks whether those six can be summarised by fewer new variables, called components, without losing much information. Each component is a weighted combination of the six: the first captures as much of the variation between households as possible, the second captures as much of what is left as possible while being uncorrelated with the first, and so on. If the six variables overlap, a few components carry most of the information, which makes the households easier to describe and to plot.

10.1 Is PCA worth doing on these variables?

PCA can only compress variables that move together. If the six were unrelated, every component would carry about the same share and nothing would be gained.

pca_cor <- soap_prep |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  cor()

# The strongest pair, and each variable's largest correlation with any other
top_pair <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(var1 < var2) |>                       # each pair once, no diagonal
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 1)

loner <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  pivot_longer(-variable, names_to = "other", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(variable != other) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(max_abs_r = max(abs(r))) |>
  slice_min(max_abs_r, n = 1)

as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(-variable, decimals = 2) |>
  data_color(columns = -variable,
             palette = c(pal_lo, "#F9E1EB", pal_hi),
             domain = c(-1, 1), autocolor_text = FALSE)

Table 31 shows the correlations. The strongest relationship is between NoTrans and TotalVol (r = 0.64), so there is real overlap for PCA to use. At the other extreme, PurOtherPromo is almost independent of the rest (its largest correlation with any other variable is 0.13), so it cannot be folded into the others and is likely to need a component of its own.

10.2 Running the PCA

The PCA follows the tidymodels recipe pattern (Kuhn and Wickham 2020; Kuhn et al. 2026): a recipe with step_normalize() and step_pca(), estimated with prep(), and checked against base R’s prcomp().

pca_data <- soap_prep |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars))

pca_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = pca_data) |>
  # keep the ID, but leave it out of the PCA
  update_role(MemberID, new_role = "id") |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>     # see the note below
  # keep all six for now
  step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = length(cluster_vars),
           id = "pca") |>
  prep()

# What step_normalize learned: for already standardised data, means are 0 and
# sds are 1
norm_check <- tidy(pca_rec, number = 1) |>
  group_by(statistic) |>
  summarise(furthest = max(abs(value - if_else(statistic == "mean", 0, 1))))

# Cross-check against base R: prcomp() should give the same variances
pca_base <- prcomp(select(pca_data, all_of(cluster_vars)))

Is step_normalize() needed again? PCA must be run on standardised data, otherwise the variable with the largest units (volume) would dominate the first component only because its numbers are bigger. soap_prep was already standardised in Section 7, so this step changes nothing here: the means it learned differ from 0, and the standard deviations from 1, by at most 6e-15, which is rounding error. It is kept so that the recipe is safe on its own if it is ever run on unprepared data. All six components are kept at this stage so that the number to retain is chosen from the evidence below rather than fixed in advance.

10.3 How many components to keep

pca_var <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "variance") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  transmute(component,
            eigenvalue = variance,
            percent    = `percent variance`,
            cumulative = `cumulative percent variance`)

# The variances match base R's prcomp() (eigenvalue = sd squared)
same_as_prcomp <- isTRUE(all.equal(pca_var$eigenvalue, pca_base$sdev^2,
                                   check.attributes = FALSE))

pca_var |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(eigenvalue, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(c(percent, cumulative), decimals = 1, pattern = "{x}%") |>
  cols_label(component = "Component", eigenvalue = "Eigenvalue",
             percent = "Variance explained", cumulative = "Cumulative")
# Kaiser: eigenvalue above 1
n_kaiser <- sum(pca_var$eigenvalue > 1)
# enough components for 70% of the variation
n_70     <- which(pca_var$cumulative >= 70)[1]
# the decision (explained below)
n_keep   <- n_70

scree <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, eigenvalue)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(colour = pal[1]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = component <= n_keep), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  labs(title = "Scree plot", x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue")

cumul <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, cumulative / 100)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = component <= n_keep), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative variance explained", x = "Component", y = NULL)

scree + cumul
eig      <- pca_var$eigenvalue
cum_keep <- pca_var$cumulative[n_keep]

Table 32 and Figure 15 show the variance explained. The first component explains 36.4% of the variation on its own, and each further component adds less. Three rules were read together to decide how many to keep:

  1. Kaiser rule (Kaiser 1960) (keep components with an eigenvalue above 1, meaning the component carries more information than a single standardised variable): 3 components.
  2. Share of variance (keep enough components to explain at least 70% of the variation): 3 components, together explaining 74%. The unit’s PCA lecture suggests that more than 60% is enough for social science data such as household purchases (ETW2500 Teaching Team 2026), so 70% is the stricter of the two and both are met.
  3. Scree plot (keep the components before the curve flattens): after component 3 the eigenvalues drop to 0.67 and 0.64, which are almost level, so the curve flattens there.

The three rules agree, so 3 components are retained, keeping 74% of the information while reducing six variables to three dimensions. One caution: the third eigenvalue is 1.008, only just above 1, so the Kaiser rule alone would be a weak reason to keep it; the share of variance and the scree plot are what make the case. As a check, base R’s prcomp() gives exactly the same eigenvalues.

10.4 Naming and describing the components

The loadings are the weights each original variable gets in a component. A loading far from 0 (here beyond <U+00B1>0.4, a common cut-off) means the variable helps define that component, and its sign says whether the variable rises or falls as the component score rises. The sign of a whole component is arbitrary in PCA (multiplying every loading by -1 describes the same component), so each component is flipped, where needed, so that its largest loading is positive and “a high score” reads naturally. Figure 16 and Table 33 show the loadings of the retained components.

kept_pcs <- paste0("PC", seq_len(n_keep))

pca_load_raw <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "coef") |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  select(variable = terms, component, value)

# Flip each component so its largest loading is positive (direction only, the
# PCA is unchanged)
pc_flip <- pca_load_raw |>
  group_by(component) |>
  slice_max(abs(value), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(component, flip = sign(value))

pca_load <- pca_load_raw |>
  left_join(pc_flip, by = "component") |>
  mutate(value  = value * flip,
         strong = abs(value) >= 0.4)

pca_load |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_rev(factor(variable, levels = cluster_vars)),
             fill = strong)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.4, 0.4), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey55") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(component, levels = kept_pcs)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Defines the component",
                               `FALSE` = "Weak")) +
  labs(title = "Loadings of the retained components", x = "Loading", y = NULL,
       fill = NULL)
pca_load_wide <- pca_load |>
  select(variable, component, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(factor(variable, levels = cluster_vars))

load_gt <- pca_load_wide |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(all_of(kept_pcs), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable")

# Bold the loadings that define each component
for (pc in kept_pcs) {
  load_gt <- load_gt |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", color = pal[1]),
              locations = cells_body(columns = all_of(pc),
                                     rows = which(abs(pca_load_wide[[pc]]) >=
                                                  0.4)))
}
load_gt
# Loading of one variable on one component, and a component's share, as text
loading_text <- \(v, pc) {
  sprintf("%+.2f", pca_load_wide[[pc]][pca_load_wide$variable == v])
}
pct_var <- \(pc) {
  round(pca_var$percent[pca_var$component == as.integer(sub("PC", "", pc))], 1)
}

PC1: Shopping activity and brand variety (36.4% of the variation). It is defined by NoTrans (+0.60), NoBrands (+0.50) and TotalVol (+0.45), so a high PC1 score means a household that buys often, buys a lot and spreads its purchases across many brands, while a low score is a light, occasional buyer. Because the number of brands loads together with the activity variables, buying more goes with trying more brands: in these data the heaviest buyers are not the most loyal ones (MaxBrShare loads -0.29).

PC2: Loyal bulk buying versus promotion seeking (20.7% of the variation). It is defined by MaxBrShare (+0.58) and TotalVol (+0.51) against PurPromo6 (-0.58). A high PC2 score means a household that puts most of its volume on one brand and buys in quantity without needing a deal; a low score means a household whose purchases lean on promotion 6. This is the loyalty versus deal-seeking axis in the Key Problem, and it is a different idea from how active a household is (PC1). The word “bulk” needs care, because TotalVol also loads +0.45 on PC1. So part of the volume difference between households is already counted as activity in PC1, and because the components are uncorrelated, the volume part of PC2 is the part of volume that PC1 does not already explain.

PC3: Response to other promotions (16.8% of the variation). It is almost entirely PurOtherPromo (+0.95), the variable that was barely related to any other. It earns a component of its own because this kind of promotion response is separate from both activity and loyalty: knowing how much a household buys, or how loyal it is, says little about whether it takes up these offers.

10.5 The households on the components

Each household gets a score on every retained component. Plotting the first two scores shows the households in two dimensions instead of six, coloured by their segment from Question 2, with the loadings drawn as arrows pointing in the direction in which each variable increases.

# Component scores, flipped the same way as the loadings, joined to the segments
pca_scores <- bake(pca_rec, new_data = NULL) |>
  select(MemberID, all_of(kept_pcs)) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(kept_pcs),
                \(x) x * pc_flip$flip[pc_flip$component == cur_column()])) |>
  left_join(soap_clusters |> select(MemberID, segment), by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_names))

# Arrows: the PC1 and PC2 loadings, stretched so they are visible next to the
# scores
arrow_scale <- 0.8 * max(abs(c(pca_scores$PC1, pca_scores$PC2)))
pca_arrows  <- pca_load |>
  filter(component %in% c("PC1", "PC2")) |>
  select(variable, component, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(c(PC1, PC2), \(x) x * arrow_scale))

ggplot(pca_scores, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = segment), alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(data = pca_arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), colour = pal_ink) +
  geom_label(data = pca_arrows, aes(label = variable), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Households on the first two components",
       x = "PC1: Shopping activity and brand variety",
       y = "PC2: Loyal bulk buying versus promotion seeking", colour = NULL)
# Mean score per segment, and R squared of each component's scores on segment
seg_means <- pca_scores |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(kept_pcs), mean)) |>
  mutate(segment = as.character(segment))

seg_r2 <- map_dbl(kept_pcs, \(pc) summary(lm(reformulate("segment", pc),
                                             data = pca_scores))$r.squared) |>
  set_names(kept_pcs)

seg_means |>
  bind_rows(tibble(segment = "Variation explained by segment",
                   PC1 = seg_r2[["PC1"]], PC2 = seg_r2[["PC2"]],
                   PC3 = seg_r2[["PC3"]])) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(all_of(kept_pcs),
             rows = segment != "Variation explained by segment",
             decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(all_of(kept_pcs),
              rows = segment == "Variation explained by segment",
              decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment")
seg_score <- \(seg, pc) sprintf("%+.2f",
                                seg_means[[pc]][seg_means$segment == seg])

Figure 17 plots the households and Table 34 gives each segment’s mean score. The plot reads like a map of the segments. Moving right (PC1) goes from the Light occasional buyers (-3.18) to the Heavy multi-brand shoppers (+1.48), the two ends of shopping activity. Moving up (PC2) goes from the Promo-6 buyers at the bottom (-1.37) to the Loyal regular-price buyers (+0.93) and Loyal promotion buyers (+0.89) at the top, the loyalty against deal-seeking axis. The MaxBrShare and PurPromo6 arrows point in opposite directions, so households that are loyal to one brand tend not to rely on promotion 6. PC3, not shown in the plot, is where the Loyal promotion buyers stand out (+1.98), because they are the segment that takes up other promotions.

Segment membership explains 62% of the variation in PC1, 54% in PC2 and 42% in PC3. The PCA therefore agrees with the clustering and names the dimensions behind it: the clustering finds the groups, and the components name the three dimensions on which they differ, which are activity, loyalty against promotion 6, and response to other promotions. This is not independent proof that the segments are real, because both methods use the same six prepared variables.

10.6 What PCA gives up

PCA kept 74% of the information, so 26% of the variation between households is set aside. Three further limits matter for a client:

  • Components are harder to explain than the original variables. “Shopping activity and brand variety” is a weighted mix of several variables, and a manager may find “number of transactions” easier to act on. This is why the segments in Question 2 were described with the original variables.
  • PCA only finds straight-line relationships, and is pulled by extreme values. The skew correction and standardisation in Section 7 reduce this, but a curved pattern, or one driven by a small group of heavy promotion users, can be missed or exaggerated.
  • It cannot compress variables that do not overlap. PurOtherPromo was nearly unrelated to the others, so it needed a component to itself. When most variables are unrelated, PCA saves little; it is most useful when many variables measure a few underlying ideas.

11 Conclusion and Recommendations

11.1 What we found

XYZ asked whether the bath soap market could be segmented by how households buy rather than by who they are. It can. Question 1 showed that raw brand shares measure which brand a household buys, not how loyal it is, so they were replaced by a single concentration measure, MaxBrShare. Six behaviour variables covering volume, frequency, promotion response and loyalty were then cleaned, corrected for skewness and standardised (Section 7), and Ward’s hierarchical clustering grouped the 600 households into six segments (Section 8).

The PCA in Section 10 agrees with the clustering and names the dimensions behind it. It is not independent proof, since both use the same six variables. Three components keep 74% of the information: shopping activity and brand variety, loyal bulk buying against promotion 6, and response to other promotions. Segment membership explains 62%, 54% and 42% of the variation in these three components, so the segments line up with clear, nameable dimensions of behaviour rather than with noise.

The demographic profile in Section 9 adds one important lesson: the segments are only weakly visible in demographics. Socioeconomic class and household size differ between segments, but the effects are small, and age does not differ at all. A client could not have found these segments from demographics, which is exactly why XYZ’s move to behavioural segmentation is worthwhile.

11.2 Recommendations for XYZ’s clients

recommendations <- tribble(
  ~segment, ~what_defines_it, ~recommended_approach,
  "Loyal regular-price buyers",
  "Most volume on one brand, almost no promotion buying",
  str_c("Reward and loyalty schemes to keep them; avoid discounts, which ",
        "only give away margin"),
  "Loyal promotion buyers",
  "The most loyal segment, and heavy users of other promotions",
  "Price promotions and value packs on the brand they already favour",
  "Heavy multi-brand shoppers",
  "The most volume and transactions, spread across many brands",
  str_c("Family and multi-packs tied to one brand, with rewards that ",
        "concentrate their spending"),
  "Promo-6 buyers",
  "Low loyalty, heavy use of promotion 6, more higher-class households",
  "Promotion 6 offers spread across the year; a cheaper product is not needed",
  "Small-brand regular-price buyers",
  str_c("Average volume, little spent on the eight named brands, rarely ",
        "buys on promotion"),
  str_c("Trial and visibility to win them from small brands; discounts are ",
        "unlikely to move them. The least sharply defined segment, so test ",
        "on a small scale first"),
  "Light occasional buyers",
  "Very low volume, few transactions, poorly recorded demographics",
  "Lowest priority for promotion spending"
) |>
  mutate(households = map_int(segment, seg_size), .after = segment)

recommendations |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             what_defines_it = "What defines it",
             recommended_approach = "Recommended approach") |>
  cols_width(segment ~ px(170), households ~ px(90))

The segments differ in when and how a promotion pays off, which is what lets a client spread several promotions across the year instead of one blanket discount. Table 35 sets out one approach per segment. The two loyal segments together hold 176 households, and they need opposite treatment: one should be rewarded without discounts, the other responds to discounts on its own brand. Treating them as one “loyal” group, as a demographic segmentation would, would waste the promotion budget on the first and under-serve the second.

11.3 Limitations

  • The segments overlap. The average silhouette width at six clusters is only 0.158, and the adjusted Rand index against k-means is 0.389 (Section 8.3.2). The overlap is uneven: the average silhouette width is 0.467 for the Light occasional buyers but only 0.073 for the Small-brand regular-price buyers, so households near the borders of the weaker segments could reasonably belong to a neighbouring one.
  • Six groups is partly a judgement. The silhouette slightly favours two groups; six was chosen because two would mix loyal and light buyers, which no client could act on (Section 8.2).
  • Data quality. Demographics coded 0 were treated as missing, and CHILD = 5 was treated as an undocumented “not specified” code. 2 households have brand shares that do not sum to 1, and the largest share of the 68 households with no household size (and no education, language, gender, TV or Affluence) sits in the Light occasional segment.
  • Skewness in the promotion shares remains. About half the households never use each promotion, so even after the square root the promotion shares stay skewed. This reflects real behaviour but makes those variables less symmetric than the others.
  • One sample, one period, no causation. The analysis uses a subset of 600 households over a single period. The recommendations describe which promotion fits each segment’s behaviour; they do not prove that a promotion causes a change, which only a controlled test could show.

11.4 Next steps

  1. Run the same segmentation on the full panel and on a later period, to check that the six segments are stable and to see which households move between them.
  2. Test the recommended promotions with a controlled trial in one market before rolling them out, so their effect on each segment can be measured.
  3. Consider a brand switching measure that is not built from NoTrans, which Section 6 showed is the problem with BrandRuns and TransPerRun, to capture the third view of loyalty in the brief.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false" .exec-summary}
## Executive summary

- **Six behavioural segments.** Ward's hierarchical clustering on six purchase variables (volume, frequency, two promotion shares, number of brands and `MaxBrShare`) splits the households into Small-brand regular-price buyers, Heavy multi-brand shoppers, Loyal regular-price buyers, Promo-6 buyers, Loyal promotion buyers and Light occasional buyers (sizes in @tbl-segment-means).
- **Loyalty is measured as concentration, not brand.** Raw brand shares would group households by *which* brand they buy; the single variable `MaxBrShare` measures *how concentrated* their buying is, which is what loyalty means (Question 1).
- **Three dimensions name the segments.** PCA keeps three components (@tbl-pca-variance): shopping activity and brand variety, loyal bulk buying against promotion 6, and response to other promotions. The segments line up with these dimensions (@tbl-pca-segments), which agrees with the clustering but is not independent proof, since both use the same six variables.
- **Demographics barely separate the segments.** Socioeconomic class and household size differ only slightly and age not at all, so clients should target these segments with purchase data, using demographics only to fine-tune.
- **One approach per segment.** Rewards without discounts for the Loyal regular-price buyers, price promotions on the brand they already favour for the Loyal promotion buyers, brand-tied multi-packs for the Heavy multi-brand shoppers, well-timed promotion 6 offers for the Promo-6 buyers, trial and visibility for the Small-brand regular-price buyers, and the lowest priority for the Light occasional buyers. The main caution is that segment borders overlap, and some segments are much sharper than others (@sec-robust).
:::

## Business problem

XYZ is an Asian market research agency that tracks the purchase behaviour of household panels across more than 100 cities and towns. Its clients are advertising agencies, which use the data to advise on advertising and promotion, and consumer goods manufacturers, which use it to monitor market share. Until now XYZ has segmented markets by purchaser *demographics*. This report segments the bath soap market by purchase *behaviour* instead: how much a household buys (volume), how often it buys (frequency), how strongly it responds to discounts (promotion sensitivity) and how loyal it is to a brand.

Segmenting on behaviour matters commercially because a promotion aimed at the right group is cheaper than one aimed at everyone. If households that only buy on discount can be told apart from households that are loyal to one brand, a client can run several different promotions at different times of the year, and can design reward schemes that deepen brand loyalty where it already exists. The demographics are then used afterwards to *profile* each behavioural segment, which shows who the segments are.

## Objectives

This report answers three questions on a panel of households:

1. **Question 1, brand loyalty.** Why raw brand shares are a poor basis for measuring loyalty, and how to replace them with a single variable, `MaxBrShare`.
2. **Question 2, segmentation.** Select behavioural variables, prepare them, group the households with cluster analysis, describe each group and profile the groups with demographics.
3. **Question 3, dimension reduction.** Summarise the six segmentation variables into a smaller number of components with principal component analysis.

## Approach

The analysis runs in one line of dependencies. The loyalty variable `MaxBrShare` (Question 1) feeds the choice of six behaviour variables (Question 2a). Those six are cleaned, corrected for skewness and standardised (Question 2b). The prepared data are then clustered and the groups described (Question 2c and 2d) and profiled with demographics (Question 2e). The same six prepared variables are also summarised by principal component analysis (Question 3).


# How to Reproduce This Report {#sec-reproduce}

Every result in this report is calculated by the visible code from the two data files supplied. Follow these steps to rebuild it from the submitted project.

1. **Unzip the project and keep its layout.** The folder contains `ErwynaSooW.Rproj`, a `dataset/` folder (`bathsoap.csv` and `brand_example.csv`) and a `document/` folder (`ErwynaSooW.qmd`, its rendered HTML and PDF, the bibliography and the stylesheet). Do not move or rename any file.

2. **Install the software.** You need R and the Quarto CLI. RStudio and VS Code are alternative editors. The versions that produced this report are in @tbl-reproduction-software. Package versions are listed in the [appendix](#sec-appendix).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reproduction-software
#| tbl-cap: "Software versions used to render this report."

knitr::kable(tibble::tibble(
  Software = c("R", "Quarto CLI", "Platform"),
  Version  = c(as.character(getRversion()),
               trimws(system2("quarto", "--version", stdout = TRUE)),
               R.version$platform)
))
```

3. **Open the project root.** In RStudio, open `ErwynaSooW.Rproj` first. In VS Code, use **File > Open Folder** to open the folder containing that file, then open a terminal in that folder. This gives `here()` the project root it uses to find `dataset/`. Do not move or rename the data files.

4. **Prepare the packages once.** In an R console, install the bootstrap and rendering packages with `install.packages(c("pacman", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "ragg"), repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")`. The shared setup uses `pacman::p_load()` and `p_install()` to install any other missing package (`tidyverse`, `tidymodels`, `here`, `janitor`, `gt`, `scales`, `patchwork`, `factoextra`, `cluster`, `moments`, `mclust`), so the first render needs internet access and a writable R library. Figures use the `ragg` device.

5. **Render both required formats.** Open `document/ErwynaSooW.qmd` in RStudio and use the **Render** dropdown to select each format, or run these commands in a terminal at the project root:

```bash
quarto render document/ErwynaSooW.qmd --to html
quarto render document/ErwynaSooW.qmd --to typst
```

   The outputs are `document/ErwynaSooW.html` (the main document) and `document/ErwynaSooW.pdf` (the attachment). The PDF uses Typst, so no LaTeX installation is needed. The single render command without `--to` also produces both formats in the Quarto version recorded above.

6. **Repeatable results.** The setup chunk sets `set.seed(55789)`, the last five digits of the group leader's student ID. Hierarchical clustering and PCA are not random, so the seed only matters for the simulated p-values and the k-means check, which uses random starts. Keeping the code, data, package versions, seed and order of random operations fixed makes the numerical results repeatable.

7. **If something fails.** If `quarto` is not recognised, install the Quarto CLI, add its `bin` folder to `PATH`, and reopen your editor or terminal. If a package fails to install, run `install.packages("name")` once and render again. If a data file cannot be found, check that you opened the `.Rproj` file and that the `dataset/` folder sits next to it.


# Setup and Data {#sec-setup}

## Packages, seed and theme

All packages are loaded in one chunk, before anything else runs. `pacman::p_load()` installs any package that is missing on the reader's machine, so the report renders without a separate installation step. There is no `install.packages()` call anywhere in this document. The analysis is written in R [@rcore2026] with the tidyverse [@wickham2019tidyverse] for data handling and graphics and tidymodels [@kuhn2020tidymodels; @R-recipes] for the preparation and PCA recipes. Clustering uses `cluster` [@R-cluster] and `factoextra` [@R-factoextra], tables use `gt` [@R-gt], paths use `here` [@R-here], cleaning uses `janitor` [@R-janitor], combined figures use `patchwork` [@R-patchwork], the adjusted Rand index comes from `mclust` [@scrucca2016mclust] and skewness from `moments` [@R-moments].

```{r}
#| label: setup

# pacman installs anything missing, then loads it
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, tidymodels, here, janitor, gt, scales, patchwork,
       factoextra, cluster, moments)
# mclust is installed but not attached: its map() would hide purrr::map(),
# so it is called as mclust::adjustedRandIndex()
p_install(mclust, force = FALSE)

# The seed is the last five digits of the group leader's student ID.
# Clustering and any random split depend on it, so setting it once, here,
# makes every result in this report repeat exactly.
set.seed(55789)

# One flat purple and pink palette and one chart theme for the whole report, so every
# figure matches the HTML styling (document/style.css uses the same colours).
# pal[1] is the main colour and pal[4] its opposite in the diverging scales.
pal      <- c("#8A77DD", "#F28DB5", "#7DB3E8", "#F1CF68", "#8FD3BD", "#C9A0E8")
pal_grey <- "#D9D3EA"   # neutral, for "not selected" bars
pal_ink  <- "#34304A"   # text and arrows
pal_lo   <- "#A9CDF0"   # light ends of the diverging scales, so dark text
pal_hi   <- "#E7A0C0"   # stays readable on top of every cell
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = pal_ink),
          text = element_text(colour = pal_ink),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = "#6B6680"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#ECE6F7"),
          legend.position = "bottom")
)
```

## Reading the data

The file `bathsoap.csv` has one row per household. `brand_example.csv` is the three household toy example used in Question 1. Both are read with `here()`, which builds the path from the project root (the folder that holds `ErwynaSooW.Rproj`), so the paths work on any computer.

```{r}
#| label: load-data

soap_raw      <- read_csv(here("dataset", "bathsoap.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)
brand_example <- read_csv(here("dataset", "brand_example.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)

# Column groups, named once so every section uses the same definitions.
# The eight named brands are used for loyalty; BrOthers pools many small brands
# and is deliberately left out of that list (see Question 1).
brand_cols <- c("Br57_144", "Br55", "Br272", "Br286", "Br24", "Br481",
                "Br352", "Br5")
demo_cols  <- c("SEC", "FEH", "MT", "SEX", "AGE", "EDU", "HS", "CHILD", "CS",
                "Affluence")
```

## First look

```{r}
#| label: tbl-first-look
#| tbl-cap: "Basic checks on bathsoap.csv."

# Households whose nine brand shares do not add up to 1 within 0.01.
# Defined once here so other sections can reuse it.
share_exceptions <- soap_raw |>
  mutate(share_total = rowSums(pick(all_of(brand_cols), BrOthers))) |>
  filter(abs(share_total - 1) >= 0.01) |>
  select(MemberID, share_total)

tibble(
  households        = nrow(soap_raw),
  columns           = ncol(soap_raw),
  unique_ids        = n_distinct(soap_raw$MemberID),
  missing_cells     = sum(is.na(soap_raw)),
  shares_off        = nrow(share_exceptions)
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(households = "Households", columns = "Columns",
             unique_ids = "Unique IDs", missing_cells = "Empty cells (NA)",
             shares_off = "Brand shares not summing to 1 (within 0.01)")
```

@tbl-first-look shows that the data have `r nrow(soap_raw)` households and no empty cells, and all but `r nrow(share_exceptions)` households have nine brand shares that add up to 1 within 0.01 (the exceptions are listed in @tbl-q1b-share-exceptions). A clean-looking table does **not** mean there is no missing information. The data guide says a code of 0 means "not specified" for the demographic variables, so the missing values are hidden inside the numbers. @sec-prep finds and handles them.


# Question 1, Part A: Thinking About Brand Loyalty {#sec-q1a}

Before any calculation, this part asks what brand loyalty actually is, and whether the nine brand share columns measure it. The answer decides how the loyalty variable is built in @sec-q1b and which variables enter the segmentation in @sec-q2a.

## Loyalty of households X and Y (item 1)

Household X buys only brand A and household Y buys only brand B. The two households are **equally loyal**. Each puts 100% of its purchases into a single brand, so neither splits its loyalty across alternatives.

Brand loyalty therefore depends on **how concentrated a household's purchases are**, not on **which brand** receives them. Two things carry that information:

- **Share:** the proportion of a household's volume that goes to its most purchased brand. A share of 1 is complete loyalty and a share of 0.5 is a household that divides itself between two brands.
- **Concentration:** how many brands the volume is spread over. The fewer the brands, and the more uneven the split, the more loyal the household.

The name of the brand is irrelevant. A household that gives 90% of its volume to brand A and a household that gives 90% to brand B are the same kind of customer, and a client would use the same retention promotion on both.

## Euclidean distances between X, Y and Z (item 2)

Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squared differences across the variables. Here the variables are the two brand shares, so the distance between households $i$ and $j$ is $\sqrt{(A_i - A_j)^2 + (B_i - B_j)^2}$. A small distance means the two households look alike to a distance based method.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-example-distances
#| tbl-cap: "Euclidean distance between households X, Y and Z."

# dist() needs numbers only, so the Household names move into the row names.
# as.data.frame() first, because tibbles do not keep row names.
example_shares <- brand_example |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  column_to_rownames("Household")

# Euclidean distance between every pair of rows (the default method of dist())
example_dist <- dist(example_shares, method = "euclidean")

# Turn the dist object into a square table with the household names restored
as.matrix(example_dist) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "Household") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = -Household, decimals = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-example-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "Each pair of toy households, from closest to furthest."

# One row per pair (each pair once), sorted from closest to furthest
example_pairs <- as.matrix(example_dist) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "from") |>
  pivot_longer(-from, names_to = "to", values_to = "distance") |>
  filter(from < to) |>
  arrange(distance)

example_pairs |>
  mutate(pair = str_c(from, " and ", to)) |>
  select(pair, distance) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = distance, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(pair = "Pair of households", distance = "Euclidean distance")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-geometry
#| fig-cap: "Households X, Y and Z by brand share. Every household whose two shares add up to 1 lies on the dashed line."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Straight line segments between each pair, labelled with their distance
segment_tbl <- example_pairs |>
  left_join(rename(brand_example, from = Household, x1 = BrandA, y1 = BrandB),
            by = "from") |>
  left_join(rename(brand_example, to = Household, x2 = BrandA, y2 = BrandB),
            by = "to") |>
  # Label at the midpoint, moved off the line for the longest pair so it does
  # not cover Z
  mutate(label_x = (x1 + x2) / 2 + if_else(distance == max(distance), 0.18, 0),
         label_y = (y1 + y2) / 2 + if_else(distance == max(distance), 0.18, 0))

ggplot(brand_example, aes(BrandA, BrandB)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = -1, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(data = segment_tbl, aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2),
               colour = pal[2], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_label(data = segment_tbl,
             aes(x = label_x, y = label_y, label = round(distance, 3)),
             size = 3.5, colour = pal_ink) +
  geom_point(size = 5, colour = pal[1]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Household), nudge_x = 0.04, nudge_y = 0.05,
            fontface = "bold") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.1, 1.15), ylim = c(-0.1, 1.15)) +
  labs(title = "X and Y are furthest apart, yet equally loyal",
       x = "Share of volume in brand A", y = "Share of volume in brand B")
```

@tbl-example-distances gives the full distance matrix and @tbl-example-pairs ranks the pairs. The closest pairs are `r str_c("(", example_pairs$from[example_pairs$distance == min(example_pairs$distance)], ", ", example_pairs$to[example_pairs$distance == min(example_pairs$distance)], ")", collapse = " and ")`, tied at `r sprintf("%.3f", min(example_pairs$distance))`, while X and Y are the furthest apart at `r sprintf("%.3f", max(example_pairs$distance))`. Household Z splits its volume evenly between the two brands, so it sits halfway between X and Y and is the same distance from each.

**This is not consistent with item 1.** In item 1, X and Y are equally loyal, so they should be the most similar pair on loyalty. The distances say the opposite: X and Y are the most different pair, and each looks more like the half and half household Z. The distance is reading *which brand* was bought, and is blind to *how concentrated* the buying is.

The geometry shows why. Every household with two shares that add up to 1 lies on the dashed line in @fig-example-geometry, and distance along that line measures how far apart two households are in brand choice. A household with shares 0.9 and 0.1 would sit very close to X (a distance of `r sprintf("%.3f", sqrt(0.1^2 + 0.1^2))`) and far from Y (`r sprintf("%.3f", sqrt(0.9^2 + 0.9^2))`), even though a 90% concentration is nearly as loyal as Y's 100%.

## Using the nine brand shares unchanged (item 3)

Distance based methods such as cluster analysis group households that are close together, so they will inherit the problem in item 2. If the nine brand share variables (eight named brands and `BrOthers`) enter the analysis unchanged, three things go wrong.

1. **Households group by the brand they buy, not by how loyal they are.** Two households that each give all of their volume to a single brand have a squared distance of exactly 2 if the brands differ, and 0 if the brands are the same. So fully loyal households form one tight group per brand and sit far from each other, even though they behave identically.
2. **Loyalty gets far too much weight.** Nine of the columns would describe brand choice, so one idea (loyalty) would outvote volume, frequency and promotions, which would each be a single column.
3. **The nine shares are not independent.** They add up to 1 (for all but `r nrow(share_exceptions)` households, see @sec-q1b), so any one is almost fixed by the other eight. A distance method counts the same information nine times over.

### Extra check: the same problem on the real data

The question only asks for an explanation. This check goes further and tests the claim on the real data, using only the households that put **all** of their volume into one named brand.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nine-share-distances
#| tbl-cap: "Fully loyal households: the distance on the nine shares depends only on the brand."

# The nine share columns: eight named brands plus the pooled BrOthers
nine_cols <- c(brand_cols, "BrOthers")

# Households that put all of their volume into one single named brand.
# max.col() finds, for each row, the column (brand) that holds the largest
# share.
loyal <- soap_raw |>
  # near(): safe comparison for decimals
  filter(if_any(all_of(brand_cols), \(x) near(x, 1))) |>
  mutate(brand = brand_cols[max.col(across(all_of(brand_cols)),
                                    ties.method = "first")])

# Pairwise Euclidean distance on the nine shares, kept as a square matrix
loyal_dist <- as.matrix(dist(select(loyal, all_of(nine_cols))))

# For each pair of households, were they loyal to the same brand?
loyal_pairs <- which(upper.tri(loyal_dist), arr.ind = TRUE) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(distance = loyal_dist[cbind(row, col)],
         same_brand = loyal$brand[row] == loyal$brand[col])

loyal_pairs |>
  count(same_brand, distance = round(distance, 3)) |>
  mutate(same_brand = if_else(same_brand, "Same brand", "Different brand")) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(same_brand = "Loyal to", distance = "Distance on the nine shares",
             n = "Pairs of households")
```

@tbl-nine-share-distances groups the pairs by distance. There are `r nrow(loyal)` households that are completely loyal to one named brand, which makes `r nrow(loyal_pairs)` pairs. Every pair that shares a brand has a distance of `r sprintf("%.0f", unique(loyal_pairs$distance[loyal_pairs$same_brand]))`, because their rows are identical. Every pair with different brands has a distance of `r sprintf("%.3f", unique(round(loyal_pairs$distance[!loyal_pairs$same_brand], 3)))`, the square root of 2, and these make up `r scales::percent(mean(!loyal_pairs$same_brand), accuracy = 1)` of all pairs. Behaviour is identical in all `r nrow(loyal)` households, yet the unchanged shares push most of them as far apart as two single brand buyers can be. A clustering algorithm would split them by brand name, which a client cannot use. The brand shares have to be replaced by a variable that measures concentration and ignores identity, which is what `MaxBrShare` does in @sec-q1b.


# Question 1, Part B: Creating MaxBrShare {#sec-q1b}

## Creating the variable (item 4)

For household $i$, $\mathrm{MaxBrShare}_i = \max_{b \in B} s_{ib}$, where $B$ is the set of eight named brands and $s_{ib}$ is brand $b$'s share of that household's purchase volume. It measures how concentrated a household is on one named brand, whatever that brand is.

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-create

soap <- soap_raw |>
  # one household (row) at a time
  rowwise() |>
  # largest of the eight named shares
  mutate(MaxBrShare = max(c_across(all_of(brand_cols)))) |>
  # back to normal column operations
  ungroup()
```

The maximum is taken row by row because each household needs its own value. The maximum of a whole column would describe one brand across all households instead. `BrOthers` is excluded because it pools many small brands, so a high `BrOthers` share does not show loyalty to any single brand.

## Checking the variable (item 5)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-maxbrshare-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of MaxBrShare, and the number of brands bought by households with MaxBrShare = 0."

# Households with no volume in any of the eight named brands
zero_hh <- soap |> filter(near(MaxBrShare, 0))

# Five-number summary and mean, then the zero group as extra rows
enframe(summary(soap$MaxBrShare), name = "statistic", value = "value") |>
  mutate(value = sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(value))) |>
  bind_rows(zero_hh |>
              count(NoBrands, name = "n") |>
              transmute(statistic = paste0("MaxBrShare = 0 and ",
                                           NoBrands, " brand(s): households"),
                        value = as.character(n))) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(statistic = "Statistic", value = "Value")
```

@tbl-maxbrshare-summary checks the new variable. **`r nrow(zero_hh)` households have `MaxBrShare` = 0, and every one of them has `NoBrands` = `r paste(unique(zero_hh$NoBrands), collapse = ", ")`.** All values lie between `r min(soap$MaxBrShare)` and `r max(soap$MaxBrShare)`, as a share must. These households buy a single brand, but that brand sits inside `BrOthers`. Once `BrOthers` is excluded, all eight named shares are zero, so their maximum is zero. A zero therefore means "no concentration on a *named* brand", not "no loyalty": these households are in fact completely loyal to one small brand.

## Repeating the distance calculation (item 6)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-distance-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Euclidean distances between X, Y and Z: original shares against MaxBrShare alone."

example <- brand_example |>
  # largest share for each toy household
  mutate(MaxBrShare = pmax(BrandA, BrandB))

# Pairwise Euclidean distances for any set of columns, one row per pair
pair_dist <- function(cols) {
  m <- example |> select(all_of(cols)) |> as.matrix()
  rownames(m) <- example$Household
  as.matrix(dist(m)) |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "from") |>
    pivot_longer(-from, names_to = "to", values_to = "distance") |>
    filter(from < to)
}

dist_compare <- pair_dist(c("BrandA", "BrandB")) |>
  rename(original_shares = distance) |>
  left_join(pair_dist("MaxBrShare") |> rename(max_share = distance),
            by = c("from", "to"))

dist_compare |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(original_shares, max_share), decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(from = "Household", to = "and",
             original_shares = "Original shares (Part A)",
             max_share = "MaxBrShare alone")
```

@tbl-q1b-distance-comparison repeats the Part A distances. With the original shares, X and Y are the furthest apart (`r sprintf("%.3f", dist_compare$original_shares[dist_compare$from == "X" & dist_compare$to == "Y"])`) even though both are fully loyal. Using `MaxBrShare` alone, X and Y are `r dist_compare$max_share[dist_compare$from == "X" & dist_compare$to == "Y"]` apart, identical, and each is `r dist_compare$max_share[dist_compare$from == "X" & dist_compare$to == "Z"]` from Z, which splits its buying evenly. This fixes the problem from @sec-q1a: distance now reflects *how concentrated* buying is, not *which brand* was bought.

## Reading MaxBrShare with NoBrands (item 7)

`MaxBrShare` shows how concentrated a household is on its favourite named brand, while `NoBrands` shows how many brands it spreads across, so only together do they separate truly disloyal households from the `r nrow(zero_hh)` single-brand households whose `MaxBrShare` is zero only because their brand is in `BrOthers`.

The next three sections go beyond the question. They compute `MaxBrShare` a second way, show how concentration is spread and check the households whose shares do not sum to 1.

## Extra check: a second way to compute MaxBrShare

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-second-method

# pmax() works across whole columns at once instead of one row at a time
max_pmax <- do.call(pmax, select(soap_raw, all_of(brand_cols)))
# Stops the render if the two methods ever disagree
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(soap$MaxBrShare, max_pmax)))
n_same <- sum(near(soap$MaxBrShare, max_pmax))
```

The vectorised `pmax()` gives the same value for all `r n_same` households (the `stopifnot()` check would stop the render otherwise). It is the more efficient form because it avoids creating a group for each row. The `rowwise()` approach is kept above because it shows the row-by-row logic most clearly.

## Extra check: how concentration is spread

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1b-maxbrshare
#| fig-cap: "Left: distribution of MaxBrShare. Right: MaxBrShare against the number of brands bought (line = median at each brand count)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

p_hist <- ggplot(soap, aes(MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = pal[1],
                 colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Concentration on one named brand", x = "MaxBrShare",
       y = "Households")

p_scatter <- ggplot(soap, aes(NoBrands, MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[1], alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line", colour = pal[2], linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "More brands, less concentration", x = "Number of brands bought",
       y = "MaxBrShare")

p_hist + p_scatter
```

@fig-q1b-maxbrshare shows the spread. The middle half of households give between `r percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.25), accuracy = 1)` and `r percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.75), accuracy = 1)` of their volume to their favourite named brand, and `r sum(near(soap$MaxBrShare, 1))` give it all of their volume. Concentration falls as the number of brands rises, but households with the same brand count still differ widely, and the single-brand households include both 100% named-brand buyers and the zero group. This is why the two variables are read together.

## Extra check: do the nine shares add up to 1? {#sec-share-check}

`r nrow(soap) - nrow(share_exceptions)` households have nine shares (eight named brands plus `BrOthers`) that sum to 1 within 0.01. The `r nrow(share_exceptions)` exceptions are shown in @tbl-q1b-share-exceptions. They are kept as supplied, because rescaling them would change the measure the question defines. Their `MaxBrShare` values are still valid shares between 0 and 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-share-exceptions
#| tbl-cap: "Households whose nine brand shares do not sum to 1 (share_exceptions from @sec-setup)."

share_exceptions |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(share_total, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(MemberID = "Household ID", share_total = "Sum of the nine shares")
```


# Question 2(a): Choosing the Variables {#sec-q2a}

The segmentation should group households by **how they buy bath soap**, so only variables that describe purchase behaviour can go in. The Key Problem names four ideas: **volume**, **frequency**, **susceptibility to discounts** and **brand loyalty**. Question 3 summarises "the six variables used in Question 2", so exactly six variables are chosen: one or two for each idea, with no two that say the same thing.

## The four ideas of purchase behaviour

| Idea | Variable(s) chosen | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| Volume | `TotalVol` | The amount of soap bought in the period. It is the plain measure of how much a household buys. |
| Frequency | `NoTrans` | The number of shopping trips on which soap was bought, so it is how often a household buys. |
| Susceptibility to discounts | `PurPromo6`, `PurOtherPromo` | The share of volume bought under promotion code 6 and under any other promotion. They are the two parts of discount buying that carry separate information. |
| Brand loyalty | `MaxBrShare`, `NoBrands` | The brief names three loyalty perspectives: the number of brands bought, how often a household switches brand, and the share of spending on one brand. `NoBrands` is the first and `MaxBrShare` (built in @sec-q1b) is the third. Together they separate loyal households from those who only look disloyal. The switching perspective is discussed below. |

## Selected variables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-select-variables
#| tbl-cap: "The six clustering variables in original units."

# The six variables used for clustering (Question 2) and PCA (Question 3).
# The object name cluster_vars is used by sections 7, 8 and 10, so it must not
# change.
cluster_vars <- c("TotalVol",       # volume: total amount of soap bought
                  "NoTrans",        # frequency: number of purchase trips
                  # discounts: share of volume bought under promotion code 6
                  "PurPromo6",
                  # discounts: share bought under other promotions (PurNoPromo
                  # is the leftover)
                  "PurOtherPromo",
                  "NoBrands",       # loyalty: how many brands are bought
                  # loyalty: concentration on one named brand (Question 1)
                  "MaxBrShare")

# Quick look at the six in their original units
soap |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min,
                                      max = max))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
               # safe for names that contain "_"
               names_pattern = "(.+)_(mean|sd|min|max)") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean, sd, min, max), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", mean = "Mean", sd = "SD", min = "Minimum",
             max = "Maximum")
```

@tbl-select-variables summarises the six. They cover all four ideas. Volume and frequency have one variable each. Discounts and loyalty have two each, because in each case the two variables measure different things (the evidence is in @tbl-q2a-correlation-pairs and @fig-q2a-correlation).

## Extra check: variables that are exact copies of each other

Several columns are calculated from other columns, so they add nothing new and would count the same behaviour twice in a distance. The chunk below tests each suspected relationship on the data instead of assuming it.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q2a-redundancy
#| tbl-cap: "Columns that are exact arithmetic of other columns."

# Each row of this table is one suspected relationship, written as a function of
# the data
redundancy_checks <- tribble(
  ~relationship,                                  ~expected, ~check,
  "PurNoPromo + PurPromo6 + PurOtherPromo", 1,
    \(d) d$PurNoPromo + d$PurPromo6 + d$PurOtherPromo,
  "PrCat1 + PrCat2 + PrCat3 + PrCat4",      1,
    \(d) d$PrCat1 + d$PrCat2 + d$PrCat3 + d$PrCat4,
  "PropCat5 + ... + PropCat15",             1,
    \(d) rowSums(d[paste0("PropCat", 5:15)]),
  "Value / (TotalVol x AvgPrice / 100)",    1,
    \(d) d$Value / (d$TotalVol * d$AvgPrice / 100),
  "VolPerTrans / (TotalVol / NoTrans)",     1,
    \(d) d$VolPerTrans / (d$TotalVol / d$NoTrans),
  "TransPerRun / (NoTrans / BrandRuns)",    1,
    \(d) d$TransPerRun / (d$NoTrans / d$BrandRuns)
)

# Run every check on all households and summarise how far from the expected
# value it strays
redundancy_checks |>
  mutate(result = map(check, \(f) f(soap)),
         smallest = map_dbl(result, min),
         largest  = map_dbl(result, max)) |>
  select(relationship, expected, smallest, largest) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(smallest, largest), decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(relationship = "Relationship", expected = "Expected",
             smallest = "Smallest result", largest = "Largest result")
```

In every row the smallest and largest results sit on the expected value, to rounding error, for all `r nrow(soap)` households. This leads to four decisions:

- **The three promotion shares add up to 1**, so any one is fixed by the other two. Only two can be used, because all three would make the variables perfectly collinear (one is a copy of the other two combined). `PurNoPromo` is the one dropped, since it is the leftover.
- **`Value` is `TotalVol` times `AvgPrice`** (divided by 100), so `Value`, `TotalVol` and `AvgPrice` describe one thing in three forms. Only `TotalVol` is kept, because volume is the behaviour and `AvgPrice` and `Value` mix in the price of the brands chosen.
- **`VolPerTrans` is `TotalVol` divided by `NoTrans`**, so it is built from two variables that are already in the six.
- **`TransPerRun` is `NoTrans` divided by `BrandRuns`**, so it is a ratio of a kept variable and another that is dropped below.

## Why the others are excluded

```{r}
#| label: tbl-variable-table
#| tbl-cap: "Every column in the data: kept or dropped, and why."

# One row per column. The reason is written once per column (shared wording for
# groups).
demo_reason  <- str_c("Describes who the household is, not how it buys. ",
                      "Held back to profile the groups in Question 2(e).")
brand_reason <- str_c("The brief lists the brand shares as purchase ",
                      "behaviour, but each one measures which brand was ",
                      "bought, not how loyal the household is (Question 1 ",
                      "Part A), and the nine shares sum to 1. Replaced by ",
                      "MaxBrShare.")
prcat_reason <- str_c("Basis of purchase in the spec (a price category), not ",
                      "purchase behaviour. The four shares sum to 1, so they ",
                      "are redundant with each other.")
prop_reason  <- str_c("Basis of purchase in the spec (a selling proposition), ",
                      "not purchase behaviour. The eleven shares sum to 1, so ",
                      "they are redundant with each other.")

# Helper: correlation of two columns, as text, so no number in a reason is typed
# by hand
cor_text <- \(a, b) sprintf("%.2f", cor(soap[[a]], soap[[b]]))

variable_table <- bind_rows(
  tibble(variable = "MemberID", group = "Identifier", decision = "Dropped",
         reason = "A label for the household. It carries no behaviour."),
  tibble(variable = demo_cols, group = "Demographic", decision = "Dropped",
         reason = demo_reason),
  tribble(
    ~variable,       ~group,        ~decision, ~reason,
    "NoBrands", "Loyalty", "Kept",
    str_c("Breadth of brands bought. Read with MaxBrShare it tells loyal ",
          "buyers from those who only look disloyal (Question 1 item 7)."),
    "BrandRuns", "Loyalty", "Dropped",
    str_c("Counts runs of consecutive purchases of one brand, the switching ",
          "perspective of loyalty named in the brief. Left out because it is ",
          "strongly correlated with NoTrans (",
          cor_text("BrandRuns", "NoTrans"), ") and NoBrands (",
          cor_text("BrandRuns", "NoBrands"),
          "), so it would count frequency and breadth a second time."),
    "TotalVol", "Volume", "Kept",
    "Total volume bought. The direct measure of how much a household buys.",
    "NoTrans", "Frequency", "Kept",
    str_c("Number of purchase trips. The direct measure of how often a ",
          "household buys."),
    "Value", "Volume", "Dropped",
    str_c("Equals TotalVol times AvgPrice / 100, so it repeats volume and ",
          "adds the price of the brand chosen (correlation ",
          cor_text("Value", "TotalVol"), " with TotalVol)."),
    "TransPerRun", "Loyalty", "Dropped",
    str_c("Equals NoTrans / BrandRuns, the average length of a brand run, so ",
          "it is the other switching measure. Left out because it is built ",
          "from NoTrans, a kept variable (see the limits below); it also ",
          "overlaps with MaxBrShare (correlation ",
          cor_text("TransPerRun", "MaxBrShare"), ")."),
    "VolPerTrans", "Volume", "Dropped",
    str_c("Equals TotalVol / NoTrans, built from two variables already kept ",
          "(correlation ", cor_text("VolPerTrans", "TotalVol"),
          " with TotalVol)."),
    "AvgPrice", "Price", "Dropped",
    str_c("The brief lists it as a purchase summary, but it measures the ",
          "price level rather than one of the four ideas (volume, frequency, ",
          "discounts, loyalty). It depends on the brand and pack chosen and ",
          "it is the price part of Value."),
    "PurNoPromo", "Discounts", "Dropped",
    str_c("The leftover of the two promotion shares (all three sum to 1), ",
          "correlation ", cor_text("PurNoPromo", "PurPromo6"),
          " with PurPromo6. Using it too would add a redundant column."),
    "PurPromo6", "Discounts", "Kept",
    str_c("Share of volume under promotion code 6. Households differ widely ",
          "on it, and it is almost unrelated to PurOtherPromo."),
    "PurOtherPromo", "Discounts", "Kept",
    str_c("Share of volume under other promotions. A separate kind of ",
          "discount buying from PurPromo6.")
  ),
  tibble(variable = brand_cols, group = "Brand share", decision = "Dropped",
         reason = brand_reason),
  tribble(
    ~variable,       ~group,        ~decision, ~reason,
    "BrOthers", "Brand share", "Dropped",
    str_c("Pools many small brands, so it cannot identify loyalty to any one ",
          "brand (Question 1 Part B). Included in the nine shares that ",
          "MaxBrShare replaces."),
    "MaxBrShare", "Loyalty", "Kept",
    str_c("The largest share of volume in one named brand, built in Question ",
          "1. It measures concentration and ignores which brand was bought.")
  ),
  tibble(variable = str_c("PrCat", 1:4), group = "Price category",
         decision = "Dropped", reason = prcat_reason),
  tibble(variable = str_c("PropCat", 5:15), group = "Proposition",
         decision = "Dropped", reason = prop_reason)
)

# Safety checks: every column of the data appears once, and the kept rows are
# exactly cluster_vars
stopifnot(setequal(variable_table$variable, names(soap)),
          !anyDuplicated(variable_table$variable),
```
