```{r}
          setequal(variable_table$variable[variable_table$decision == "Kept"],
                   cluster_vars))

# Show the table in the order of the data file
variable_table |>
  mutate(order = match(variable, names(soap))) |>
  arrange(order) |>
  select(variable, group, decision, reason) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", group = "Group", decision = "Decision",
             reason = "Reason") |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(columns = decision,
                                   rows = decision == "Kept"))
```

@tbl-variable-table covers all `r nrow(variable_table)` columns (the 46 in `bathsoap.csv` plus `MaxBrShare`): `r sum(variable_table$decision == "Kept")` are kept and `r sum(variable_table$decision == "Dropped")` are dropped. The dropped columns fall into four kinds:

1. **Demographics** (`r length(demo_cols)` columns). They describe the household, not its buying, so putting them in would group households by who they are. They are kept for profiling the segments in @sec-profile, where they tell a client who each segment is.
2. **Brand shares** (nine columns). They measure which brand was bought, which @sec-q1a showed would split fully loyal households by brand name. `MaxBrShare` replaces them.
3. **Basis of purchase** (`PrCat1` to `PrCat4` and `PropCat5` to `PropCat15`, 15 columns). The spec labels these as the basis of purchase and not as purchase behaviour. Each group also sums to 1.
4. **Columns that repeat the six** (`Value`, `AvgPrice`, `VolPerTrans`, `TransPerRun`, `BrandRuns`, `PurNoPromo`). They are either arithmetic on other columns or closely related to a kept variable, so they repeat information (see @tbl-q2a-redundancy and @tbl-q2a-dropped-correlation).

## What was considered for each idea

| Idea | Winner | Considered and rejected | Why the winner is better |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volume | `TotalVol` | `Value`, `VolPerTrans` | `Value` is volume multiplied by price, so it mixes behaviour with the cost of the brand. `VolPerTrans` is built from `TotalVol` and `NoTrans`. |
| Frequency | `NoTrans` | `BrandRuns` | `NoTrans` counts every purchase transaction. `BrandRuns` counts runs of the same brand, so it tracks switching more than how often a household buys. |
| Discounts | `PurPromo6` and `PurOtherPromo` | `PurNoPromo`, one combined promotion share | `PurNoPromo` is redundant. A single combined share (1 minus `PurNoPromo`) would hide that the two promotion types are almost uncorrelated. |
| Loyalty | `MaxBrShare` and `NoBrands` | The nine brand shares, `BrOthers`, `BrandRuns`, `TransPerRun` | The nine shares measure brand identity. `MaxBrShare` measures concentration, and `NoBrands` covers the households that buy one small brand and have `MaxBrShare` of 0. `BrandRuns` and `TransPerRun` measure switching, but they overlap with `NoTrans`, `NoBrands` and `MaxBrShare` (see @tbl-q2a-dropped-correlation), so they would count the same behaviour twice. |

## Extra check: multicollinearity among the six

Multicollinearity means two variables move together so closely that they carry almost the same information. If it were present, one idea would be counted twice in every distance. The correlation heatmap checks the six before they go on.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q2a-correlation
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between the six chosen variables, in original units."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# Correlation matrix of the six, reshaped into one row per pair of variables
cor_pairs <- soap |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  cor() |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(across(c(var1, var2), \(x) factor(x, levels = cluster_vars)))

ggplot(cor_pairs, aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r), colour = abs(r) > 0.6), size = 3.6,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = pal_ink, "FALSE" = pal_ink)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal_lo, mid = "white", high = pal_hi,
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Correlation") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(cluster_vars)) +
  labs(title = "No pair of the six variables is strongly correlated", x = NULL,
       y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q2a-correlation-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "The three strongest correlations among the six chosen variables."

# Each pair once, ranked by the strength of the correlation (sign ignored)
strongest_pairs <- cor_pairs |>
  filter(as.integer(var1) < as.integer(var2)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(r))) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)

strongest_pairs |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = r, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(var1 = "Variable 1", var2 = "Variable 2", r = "Correlation")
```

The strongest correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", strongest_pairs$r[1])` between `r strongest_pairs$var1[1]` and `r strongest_pairs$var2[1]`, and **`r n_high <- sum(abs(cor_pairs$r[as.integer(cor_pairs$var1) < as.integer(cor_pairs$var2)]) > 0.7); if (n_high == 0) "no" else n_high` pairs are above 0.7**. Households that shop more often tend to try more brands, which is expected and not close to a duplicate. The two promotion shares have a correlation of only `r sprintf("%.2f", cor_pairs$r[cor_pairs$var1 == "PurPromo6" & cor_pairs$var2 == "PurOtherPromo"])`, so the two kinds of discount buying are different behaviours and both are worth keeping. `MaxBrShare` and `NoBrands` have a correlation of `r sprintf("%.2f", cor_pairs$r[cor_pairs$var1 == "NoBrands" & cor_pairs$var2 == "MaxBrShare"])`, so the two loyalty variables overlap only a little.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q2a-dropped-correlation
#| tbl-cap: "How strongly each dropped candidate is correlated with its closest chosen variable."

# Candidates that were considered and dropped, against the six that were kept
dropped_candidates <- c("Value", "VolPerTrans", "BrandRuns", "TransPerRun",
                        "AvgPrice", "PurNoPromo")

soap |>
  select(all_of(dropped_candidates), all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  cor() |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "candidate") |>
  filter(candidate %in% dropped_candidates) |>
  select(candidate, all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(cluster_vars), names_to = "closest", values_to = "r") |>
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 1, by = candidate) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(r))) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = r, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(candidate = "Dropped candidate",
             closest = "Closest chosen variable", r = "Correlation")
```

Most dropped candidates have a strong link to one of the six (`Value`, `BrandRuns`, `PurNoPromo`), or are exact arithmetic of other columns (`VolPerTrans` from two kept variables, `TransPerRun` from a kept variable and `BrandRuns`), so dropping them loses little. `AvgPrice` is the weakest case for dropping, since its correlation with the six is modest. It was dropped because the price paid per unit reflects the brand and pack size chosen rather than how the household buys, and the Key Problem names volume, frequency, discounts and loyalty and not price.

## Limits of this choice

- **The ideas are weighted unevenly.** Discounts and loyalty each have two variables and volume and frequency have one, so the segmentation gives loyalty and discounts more say in the distances. The data support this (each pair has a low correlation inside it), but a different team could weight the four ideas equally.
- **The correlations are on the original units.** Several of the six are skewed, so the preparation step in @sec-prep transforms and standardises them before clustering.
- **Switching between brands is not measured directly.** The brief names it as one of three loyalty perspectives. One rule was used for both switching measures: a column that is built from a variable already kept is dropped, whatever its correlation. `BrandRuns` counts runs inside the `NoTrans` purchase trips, and `TransPerRun` is `NoTrans` divided by `BrandRuns`, so both bring frequency back in a second time. That is why `TransPerRun` is dropped even though its correlation with `NoTrans` is only `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(soap$TransPerRun, soap$NoTrans))`, against `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(soap$BrandRuns, soap$NoTrans))` for `BrandRuns`. Switching is still reflected indirectly through `NoBrands` and `MaxBrShare`, and Question 3 fixes the count at six, so adding one would mean removing another.
- **`MaxBrShare` of 0** applies to `r sum(soap$MaxBrShare == 0)` households that buy only a brand outside the eight named. They are not disloyal, which is why `NoBrands` is in the six.


# Question 2(b): Preparing the Data {#sec-prep}

Cluster analysis groups households by distance, so the data must be ready for distance calculations. Three things can distort a distance: values hiding as real numbers (missing data coded as 0), a few huge values that stretch one variable (skewness), and variables measured on very different scales (standardisation). They are handled in that order, because each step depends on the one before.

## Step 1: Missing values hidden as zeros

The data guide gives two rules: for every demographic variable except `Affluence`, a value of 0 means "not specified", and `Affluence` is missing only when `HS` (household size) is 0. A household cannot have a size of 0, so a 0 there is also missing. @tbl-count-zeros shows how many zeros each demographic variable holds before any change.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count-zeros
#| tbl-cap: "Zeros in the demographic variables (before cleaning)."

soap |>
  summarise(across(all_of(demo_cols), \(x) sum(x == 0))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "zeros") |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Demographic variable", zeros = "Households with a 0")
```

`CHILD` has no zeros, yet the spec lists it as a demographic. Its categories run from 1 to 5, so @tbl-child-code-check checks whether category 5 behaves like a "not specified" code.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-child-code-check
#| tbl-cap: "CHILD category against HS = 0."

soap |>
  count(`HS is 0` = HS == 0, CHILD) |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: child-code-result

child5_all_hs0 <- soap |> filter(CHILD == 5) |> summarise(all(HS == 0)) |>
  pull()
child5_n       <- sum(soap$CHILD == 5)
hs0_n          <- sum(soap$HS == 0)
```

`CHILD = 5` appears in `r child5_n` households and **every one of them** has `HS = 0` (`r child5_all_hs0`), while `HS = 0` is true for `r hs0_n` households. The two flags describe the same households, so category 5 is treated as an undocumented "not specified" code for `CHILD`. This is an assumption, because the data guide does not say so, and it is recorded here so a reader can challenge it.

The next chunk applies the rules. The order matters: `Affluence` is checked against the *original* `HS` before `HS` itself has its zeros turned into `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recode-not-specified
#| tbl-cap: "Missing demographic information after recoding zeros to NA."

soap_clean <- soap |>
  mutate(
    # Affluence 0 is missing only when HS is 0. This must run BEFORE HS is
    # changed.
    Affluence = replace(Affluence, Affluence == 0 & HS == 0, NA),
    # CHILD 5 is the undocumented 'not specified' code shown above.
    CHILD     = replace(CHILD, CHILD == 5, NA),
    # For the other demographics a 0 means 'not specified' (data guide).
    across(c(SEC, FEH, MT, SEX, AGE, EDU, HS, CHILD, CS), \(x) na_if(x, 0))
  )

missing_tbl <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(all_of(demo_cols), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  mutate(percent = n_missing / nrow(soap_clean)) |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)

missing_tbl |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Demographic variable",
             n_missing = "Missing households",
             percent = "Share of households") |>
  fmt_percent(percent, decimals = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: missing-overlap

n_any_missing <- soap_clean |> mutate(m = if_any(all_of(demo_cols), is.na)) |>
  summarise(sum(m)) |> pull()
n_cs_extra    <- sum(is.na(soap_clean$CS) & !is.na(soap_clean$HS))
n_purchase_na <- soap_clean |> select(-all_of(demo_cols), -MemberID) |>
  is.na() |> sum()

# The HS = 0 block: which demographics do they still have, and how much do they
# buy?
hs0_block <- soap_clean |> filter(is.na(HS))
hs0_kept  <- demo_cols[map_lgl(demo_cols, \(v) !anyNA(hs0_block[[v]]))]
hs0_lost  <- setdiff(demo_cols, c(hs0_kept, "HS", "CHILD"))
hs0_all_lost <- all(map_lgl(hs0_lost, \(v) all(is.na(hs0_block[[v]]))))
vol_hs0   <- mean(hs0_block$TotalVol)
vol_other <- mean(soap_clean$TotalVol[!is.na(soap_clean$HS)])
```

@tbl-recode-not-specified lists what is missing after the recode. In total `r n_any_missing` households (`r percent(n_any_missing / nrow(soap_clean), accuracy = 0.1)`) have at least one demographic missing. Most of them are one block of `r hs0_n` households with no household size. These households still have `r paste(hs0_kept, collapse = " and ")` recorded, but `r paste(paste(head(hs0_lost, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(hs0_lost, 1))` are `r if (hs0_all_lost) "all missing" else "mostly missing"` and `CHILD` is the code 5, so they lack the household composition, education and television details rather than every demographic. They also buy far less soap: `r comma(vol_hs0, accuracy = 1)` units on average, against `r comma(vol_other, accuracy = 1)` for the households with a recorded size. On top of this block, `r n_cs_extra` further households have an unspecified `CS` (television availability). The purchase variables used for clustering have `r n_purchase_na` missing values.

**Decision.** The segmentation uses purchase variables only, and those are complete, so no household is dropped and nothing is imputed for the clustering. Imputing household size, education and the other missing details for these `r hs0_n` households would invent data. The demographics keep their `NA` and are used only to *profile* the groups in Question 2(e), where each variable is summarised over the households that have a value for it.

## Step 2: Skewness

Skewness measures how lopsided a distribution is. In cluster analysis a few very large values pull the mean and stretch the distance on that variable, so the groups can end up being decided by the extreme households rather than the typical ones. The six selected variables are `r paste(cluster_vars, collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-skewness-before
#| fig-cap: "The six clustering variables before any transformation."

# moments::skewness() is the third standardised moment.
# 0 is symmetric, positive means a long right tail.

soap_cluster_raw <- soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars))

skew_before <- soap_cluster_raw |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), skewness)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "skew_before")

soap_cluster_raw |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(cluster_vars), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = pal[1], colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") +
  # fewer, shorter axis labels so TotalVol's large values do not overlap
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks_extended(n = 3),
                     labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Households")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-skewness-rule
#| tbl-cap: "Skewness before transformation and the treatment chosen."

# Common rule of thumb: |skewness| above 1 is strongly skewed.
skewed_vars <- skew_before |> filter(abs(skew_before) > 1) |> pull(variable)

# Share of households with an exact zero in each variable. Promotion shares are
# often zero for households that never buy on that promotion (zero inflation).
zero_share <- soap_cluster_raw |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), \(x) mean(x == 0))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "zero_share")

# Rule used here: skewed AND at least 25% exact zeros -> square root;
# skewed with few zeros -> Yeo-Johnson; not strongly skewed -> leave alone.
sqrt_vars <- zero_share |> filter(variable %in% skewed_vars,
                                  zero_share >= 0.25) |> pull(variable)
yj_vars   <- setdiff(skewed_vars, sqrt_vars)

skew_before |>
  left_join(zero_share, by = "variable") |>
  mutate(method = case_when(variable %in% sqrt_vars ~ "Square root",
                            variable %in% yj_vars   ~ "Yeo-Johnson",
                            TRUE                    ~ "None needed")) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(skew_before, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(zero_share, decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", skew_before = "Skewness",
             zero_share = "Exact zeros", method = "Treatment")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-yj-trial
#| tbl-cap: "Trial Yeo-Johnson step on the two promotion shares: the power the recipe keeps, and the best power inside its search range."

# A trial recipe with Yeo-Johnson on the zero-heavy shares
yj_rec <- recipe(~ PurPromo6 + PurOtherPromo, data = soap_cluster_raw) |>
  step_YeoJohnson(all_predictors()) |>
  prep()
yj_kept <- tidy(yj_rec, number = 1)   # one row per variable that got a power

# The same search recipes runs (its internal objective, limits -5 to 5)
yj_best <- function(x) {
  optimize(recipes:::yj_obj, interval = c(-5, 5), maximum = TRUE,
           dat = x, ind_neg = list(is = which(x < 0), not = which(x >= 0)),
           const = sum(sign(x) * log(abs(x) + 1)), tol = 1e-4)$maximum
}

yj_trial <- tibble(variable = c("PurPromo6", "PurOtherPromo")) |>
  mutate(rows_in_tidy = map_int(variable, \(v) sum(yj_kept$terms == v)),
         best_lambda  = map_dbl(variable, \(v) yj_best(soap_cluster_raw[[v]])))

yj_trial |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(best_lambda, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", rows_in_tidy = "Powers kept by recipes",
             best_lambda = "Best power in [-5, 5]")
```

@fig-skewness-before shows the shapes and @tbl-skewness-rule the treatment chosen for each variable. Two different treatments are used, because two different problems cause the skew. Where a variable is strongly skewed but has few zeros (volume and frequency of purchase), the **Yeo-Johnson** transformation (`step_YeoJohnson()`) is used [@yeo2000]. It learns the power that makes the data most symmetric and, unlike `log()`, it accepts zeros. Where a variable is strongly skewed *and* a large share of households sit at an exact zero (the promotion shares), the **square root** (`step_sqrt()`) is used instead. A first attempt with Yeo-Johnson on those shares left them unchanged, and @tbl-yj-trial shows why. `recipes` searches for the power between -5 and 5, and for both shares the best power sits on the lower limit (`r sprintf("%.4f", min(yj_trial$best_lambda))`), so `recipes` returns no estimate and leaves the column as it is. In other words the search stops at the edge of its range rather than at a real best value. The square root is defined at zero, shrinks the long right tail and keeps the order of the households. Variables below the threshold are left alone, because a transformation that is not needed only makes the result harder to explain.

## Step 3: Standardisation

Euclidean distance adds up squared differences, so a variable measured in thousands (volume) would completely drown out one measured between 0 and 1 (a share). Standardising gives every variable a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, so each has an equal say. @tbl-scale-before shows how far apart the scales start.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scale-before
#| tbl-cap: "Scales before standardising."

soap_cluster_raw |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.+)_(mean|sd)") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(mean, sd), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", mean = "Mean", sd = "Standard deviation")
```

Both the transformation and the standardisation are done in one `recipes` recipe, so the same steps could be applied to new households later. The order is deliberate: skewness is corrected first, then the corrected values are standardised.

```{r}
#| label: prep-recipe

prep_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = soap_cluster_raw) |>
  # keep the ID, but never transform it
  update_role(MemberID, new_role = "id") |>
  step_sqrt(all_of(sqrt_vars)) |>                # zero-heavy skewed shares
  # other strongly skewed variables
  step_YeoJohnson(all_of(yj_vars)) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>    # mean 0, standard deviation 1
  # learn the lambdas, means and sds
  prep()

# the prepared data for Q2c and Q3
soap_prep <- bake(prep_rec, new_data = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-check-prepared
#| tbl-cap: "Scales after the recipe: every variable has mean 0 and standard deviation 1."

soap_prep |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.+)_(mean|sd)") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(mean, sd), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", mean = "Mean", sd = "Standard deviation")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-skewness-after
#| tbl-cap: "Skewness before and after the recipe."

# Skewness before and after. Standardising does not change skewness,
# so any change here is due to the square root and Yeo-Johnson steps.
skew_after <- soap_prep |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), skewness)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "skew_after")

skew_before |>
  left_join(skew_after, by = "variable") |>
  mutate(method = case_when(variable %in% sqrt_vars ~ "Square root",
                            variable %in% yj_vars   ~ "Yeo-Johnson",
                            TRUE                    ~ "None")) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(skew_before, skew_after), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", skew_before = "Before",
             skew_after = "After",
             method = "Treatment")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-skewness-after
#| fig-cap: "The six variables after transformation and standardising."

soap_prep |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(cluster_vars), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = pal[2], colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Standardised value", y = "Households")
```

## Step 4: Outliers

Even after the transformation, a household can sit far from the rest, and cluster methods are sensitive to such points. A standardised value beyond 3 (more than 3 standard deviations from the mean) is used as the flag. @tbl-outliers counts the flagged households and @fig-outliers shows where they sit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-outliers
#| tbl-cap: "Households beyond 3 standard deviations on each prepared variable."

outlier_tbl <- soap_prep |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), \(x) sum(abs(x) > 3))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "households_beyond_3sd")

n_outlier_hh <- soap_prep |>
  filter(if_any(all_of(cluster_vars), \(x) abs(x) > 3)) |>
  nrow()

outlier_tbl |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable",
             households_beyond_3sd = "Households with |z| > 3")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-outliers
#| fig-cap: "Boxplots of the prepared variables."

soap_prep |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(cluster_vars), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(variable, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = pal[3], outlier.colour = pal[1]) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Standardised value")
```

```{r}
#| label: prep-summary-values

sk_tab   <- skew_before |> left_join(skew_after, by = "variable")
n_flag   <- length(skewed_vars)
worst_v  <- sk_tab |> slice_max(abs(skew_after), n = 1)
fixed_v  <- sk_tab |> filter(variable %in% yj_vars)
# households extreme ONLY on the square-rooted promotion shares
n_promo_only <- soap_prep |>
  filter(if_any(all_of(cluster_vars), \(x) abs(x) > 3),
         if_all(all_of(setdiff(cluster_vars, sqrt_vars)), \(x) abs(x) <= 3)) |>
  nrow()
```

**Interpretation.** @tbl-skewness-after and @fig-skewness-after show the result. Of the six variables, `r n_flag` were strongly skewed before any treatment (|skewness| above 1). For the variables treated with Yeo-Johnson (`r paste(yj_vars, collapse = ", ")`) the skewness fell to between `r round(min(fixed_v$skew_after), 2)` and `r round(max(fixed_v$skew_after), 2)`, which is effectively symmetric. The square root helped the promotion shares (`r paste(sqrt_vars, collapse = ", ")`) but did not remove their skew; the most skewed variable after treatment is `r worst_v$variable` at `r round(worst_v$skew_after, 2)`. That remaining skew is structural rather than a flaw in the method: around half the households never buy on those promotions, so a large block sits at zero however the scale is stretched. It is therefore reported as a limitation. It also tells the clustering something real, namely that there is a group of households that never respond to promotions.

After the recipe every variable has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 (@tbl-check-prepared), so no variable dominates a distance only because of its units. Beyond three standard deviations there are `r n_outlier_hh` households (`r percent(n_outlier_hh / nrow(soap_prep), accuracy = 0.1)` of `r nrow(soap_prep)`) with at least one extreme value, and `r n_promo_only` of them are extreme only on the promotion shares. These households are **kept**. They are genuine heavy promotion users, which is exactly the behaviour a segmentation should be able to find, and removing them would hide the group a promotion-led client most wants to identify. Whether the segments depend on them is tested in @sec-robust, where they are removed and the households reclustered.


# Question 2(c) and 2(d): Clustering the Households {#sec-cluster}

## Choosing the method

The clustering method used is **agglomerative hierarchical clustering**. It works from the bottom up: each household starts as its own cluster, and at each step the two most similar clusters are combined into a bigger cluster until all households belong to one cluster. Unlike k-means, hierarchical clustering does not need the number of clusters to be fixed in advance, and its results can be shown as a dendrogram, which helps in deciding the final number of clusters.

The dissimilarity between households is measured with the **Euclidean distance**, the most commonly used distance measure. Euclidean distance needs numeric variables on a similar scale and is sensitive to outliers. These requirements were met in @sec-prep, where the six variables were skew-corrected and standardised so that no variable dominates the distance because of its larger range of values.

The linkage method is **Ward's minimum variance method** [@ward1963]. At each step it merges the pair of clusters whose merger gives the **smallest increase in the total within-cluster sum of squares**, so it tends to produce compact clusters of similar size. Single linkage was not used because it tends to chain households into long, loose clusters. Complete and average linkage were both run as a check, and @sec-robust shows why Ward's method was kept: on these data the other two leave very small or very uneven groups.

## Choosing the number of groups {#sec-choose-k}

```{r}
#| label: fig-choose-k
#| fig-cap: "Choosing the number of groups with Ward's linkage: (A) total within-cluster sum of squares and (B) average silhouette width, for 1 to 10 groups."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

# Cluster on the six variables only (MemberID is a label, not behaviour)
cluster_data <- soap_prep |> select(all_of(cluster_vars))

# Elbow and silhouette using hierarchical clustering with Ward's linkage
p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(cluster_data, FUNcluster = hcut, method = "wss",
                        k.max = 10, hc_method = "ward.D2",
                        linecolor = pal[1]) +
  labs(title = "(A) Elbow method")

p_silhouette <- fviz_nbclust(cluster_data, FUNcluster = hcut,
                             method = "silhouette",
                             k.max = 10, hc_method = "ward.D2",
                             linecolor = pal[1]) +
  labs(title = "(B) Silhouette method")

p_elbow + p_silhouette
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ward-tree
#| fig-cap: "Dendrogram of all households (Ward's linkage), cut into six groups."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Hierarchical clustering: Euclidean distance, Ward's linkage
distance_ward <- dist(cluster_data, method = "euclidean")
hc_ward <- hclust(distance_ward, method = "ward.D2")

# Number of clusters selected (justified below)
k_final <- 6

# The dendrogram cut into k_final groups, coloured with the team palette
fviz_dend(hc_ward, k = k_final, show_labels = FALSE, k_colors = pal[1:k_final],
          main = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-k-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate numbers of groups (2 to 10) compared: group sizes and average silhouette width."

# For each k, cut the Ward tree and record group sizes and average silhouette
# width
k_compare <- tibble(k = 2:10) |>
  mutate(groups = map(k, \(kk) cutree(hc_ward, k = kk)),
         sizes = map_chr(groups, \(g) paste(table(g), collapse = ", ")),
         smallest = map_int(groups, \(g) min(table(g))),
         average_silhouette = map_dbl(groups, \(g) {
           mean(silhouette(g, distance_ward)[, "sil_width"])
         }))

k_compare |>
  select(-groups) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(average_silhouette, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(k = "Groups (k)", sizes = "Households per group",
             smallest = "Smallest group",
             average_silhouette = "Average silhouette")
```

```{r}
#| label: k-values

sil_at <- \(kk) sprintf("%.3f", k_compare$average_silhouette[k_compare$k == kk])
# Best k once the two-group split is set aside, and the range for 7 to 10
best_k_3up <- k_compare |> filter(k >= 3) |> slice_max(average_silhouette) |>
  pull(k)
sil_7_10   <- range(k_compare$average_silhouette[k_compare$k >= 7])
sizes_of <- \(kk) sort(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = kk)), decreasing = TRUE)
k2 <- sizes_of(2)
# The group of five that is split in two when moving to six
split_parent <- max(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 5)))
split_kids   <- setdiff(as.integer(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 6))),
                        as.integer(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 5))))
smallest6    <- min(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 6)))
```

@fig-choose-k shows the elbow and silhouette plots, @fig-ward-tree the dendrogram and @tbl-k-compare the group sizes for each candidate. The elbow and silhouette methods do not agree on a clear number of clusters. The silhouette method favours two clusters, where the average silhouette width peaks at `r sil_at(2)`, and it falls sharply at three. However, six clusters are a close second at `r sil_at(6)`, above three, four and five clusters (`r sil_at(3)`, `r sil_at(4)` and `r sil_at(5)`) and above every choice from seven to ten (`r sprintf("%.3f", sil_7_10[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_7_10[2])`). Once two groups are set aside, the best number on the silhouette from three to ten is `r best_k_3up`. All silhouette values [@rousseeuw1987] are close to 0, which means many households lie near the border between clusters: the groups overlap rather than being sharply separated. The elbow plot does not give a clear answer either, as the largest drop is from one to two clusters and the curve flattens out after six.

**Six clusters were chosen because the clusters also need to make business sense.** The aim of the segmentation is to help XYZ's clients run several promotions, each aimed at a different segment, and to design reward schemes that build brand loyalty. Six segments is a manageable number of separate campaigns for a client to run across a year, and each segment needs a different approach: reward schemes suit loyal households, while households that buy on promotion respond to discounts. With two clusters, the Heavy multi-brand shoppers and the Promo-6 buyers form one cluster of `r k2[2]` households and everyone else forms a second cluster of `r k2[1]`. That would combine households that buy very differently, such as loyal buyers and light occasional buyers. Moving from five to six clusters splits the largest group of `r split_parent` households into `r max(split_kids)` loyal households that rarely buy on promotion and `r min(split_kids)` loyal households that buy heavily on other promotions. These behave differently and call for different promotions. More clusters would risk very small groups, but with six the smallest still holds `r smallest6` households (`r percent(smallest6 / nrow(soap_prep), accuracy = 1)` of the panel).

## The final grouping

```{r}
#| label: final-clusters

# Cut the Ward tree into k_final groups
ward_groups <- cutree(hc_ward, k = k_final)

# Names chosen from the standardised group means (see the centroid chart below)
segment_names <- c("1" = "Small-brand regular-price buyers",
                   "2" = "Heavy multi-brand shoppers",
                   "3" = "Light occasional buyers",
                   "4" = "Loyal regular-price buyers",
                   "5" = "Loyal promotion buyers",
                   "6" = "Promo-6 buyers")

# Each household's cluster and segment name, used for profiling (2e) and PCA
# (Q3)
soap_clusters <- tibble(MemberID = soap_prep$MemberID,
                        cluster  = factor(ward_groups)) |>
  mutate(segment = unname(segment_names[as.character(cluster)]))
```

Cutting the Ward dendrogram into six clusters gives segments of `r min(table(ward_groups))` to `r max(table(ward_groups))` households. Each segment was given a label based on its average values on the six variables, and each household's cluster and segment name are stored in `soap_clusters` for the rest of the analysis.

### Extra check: does the result depend on the method?

The question only asks for one clustering. This check goes further and asks whether the segments survive a different method. To check whether the segments depend on the clustering method, k-means was also run with six clusters. K-means assigns each household to the cluster with the nearest centroid, recalculates each centroid as the mean of its cluster, and repeats until the assignments stop changing. Because the starting centroids are random, k-means was run with 25 random starts, keeping the solution with the lowest total within-cluster variation, and the seed is set right before it so the result repeats exactly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ward-vs-kmeans
#| tbl-cap: "Cross table of the Ward segments (rows) against the k-means groups (columns)."

set.seed(55789)   # k-means uses random starting centroids
km_check <- kmeans(cluster_data, centers = k_final, nstart = 25)

ward_vs_km <- table(Ward = ward_groups, Kmeans = km_check$cluster)

# k-means numbers its groups differently, so agreement is read from the largest
# count in each row: the share of households in their best-matching k-means
# group
agreement     <- sum(apply(ward_vs_km, 1, max)) / length(ward_groups)
row_agreement <- apply(ward_vs_km, 1, max) / rowSums(ward_vs_km)

as.data.frame.matrix(ward_vs_km) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cluster") |>
  mutate(segment = segment_names[cluster], agreement = row_agreement) |>
  select(segment, everything(), -cluster) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(agreement, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "k-means group", columns = as.character(1:k_final)) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Ward segment", agreement = "In best-matching group")
```

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-stability

# Repeat k-means 10 times with different random starts: does the agreement hold?
stability_runs <- map_dbl(1:10, \(i) {
  km  <- kmeans(cluster_data, centers = k_final, nstart = 25)
  tab <- table(ward_groups, km$cluster)
  sum(apply(tab, 1, max)) / length(ward_groups)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-values

# Share of a segment's households in its best-matching k-means group, as text
row_agree_text <- \(seg) {
  percent(row_agreement[names(segment_names)[segment_names == seg]],
          accuracy = 1)
}
```

@tbl-ward-vs-kmeans cross-tabulates the two solutions. Overall, `r percent(agreement, accuracy = 0.1)` of households sit in their best-matching k-means group. Agreement is highest for the Light occasional buyers (`r row_agree_text("Light occasional buyers")`) and the Promo-6 buyers (`r row_agree_text("Promo-6 buyers")`), followed by the Loyal promotion buyers (`r row_agree_text("Loyal promotion buyers")`), the Loyal regular-price buyers (`r row_agree_text("Loyal regular-price buyers")`) and the Heavy multi-brand shoppers (`r row_agree_text("Heavy multi-brand shoppers")`). It is lowest for the Small-brand regular-price buyers (`r row_agree_text("Small-brand regular-price buyers")`), whose households are split across several k-means groups. This moderate agreement is consistent with the low silhouette values in @sec-choose-k: many households lie close to the border between clusters, and the Small-brand regular-price segment is the least sharply defined. Repeating k-means ten times with different random starts gave almost the same agreement each time (`r percent(min(stability_runs), accuracy = 0.1)` to `r percent(max(stability_runs), accuracy = 0.1)`), so the comparison does not depend on one particular set of starting centroids.

### Extra check: how stable are the six segments? {#sec-robust}

This section also goes beyond the question. The best-match share above flatters the agreement, because each segment is matched to whichever k-means group suits it best. These checks test the six segments more strictly. The **adjusted Rand index** (ARI) [@hubert1985] compares two groupings pair by pair: it is the share of household pairs that both groupings put together or both put apart, corrected so that 0 is the agreement expected by chance and 1 means identical groupings. It is computed with `mclust` [@scrucca2016mclust].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-robust
#| tbl-cap: "Stability checks on the six Ward segments."

# (a) best k from 3 to 10 on the silhouette (k = 2 is ruled out above)
best_sil <- k_compare$average_silhouette[k_compare$k == best_k_3up]

# (b) the same distances cut into six groups with two other linkages
linkage_sizes <- map(c(Ward = "ward.D2", Complete = "complete",
                       Average = "average"),
                     \(m) sort(table(cutree(hclust(distance_ward, method = m),
                                              k = k_final)), decreasing = TRUE))

# (c) ARI between the Ward segments and k-means
ari_kmeans <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(ward_groups, km_check$cluster)

# (d) drop households with any |z| > 3, recluster, compare on those left
keep_hh     <- rowSums(abs(cluster_data) > 3) == 0
ward_trim   <- cutree(hclust(dist(cluster_data[keep_hh, ]), method = "ward.D2"),
                      k = k_final)
ari_trimmed <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(ward_groups[keep_hh], ward_trim)

# (e) average silhouette width within each segment
sil_ward   <- silhouette(ward_groups, distance_ward)
sil_seg_of <- unname(segment_names[as.character(sil_ward[, "cluster"])])
sil_by_seg <- tibble(segment = sil_seg_of, width = sil_ward[, "sil_width"]) |>
  summarise(width = mean(width), .by = segment) |>
  arrange(desc(width))

robust_tbl <- bind_rows(
  tibble(group  = "Number of groups",
         check  = "Best k from 3 to 10 (average silhouette)",
         result = paste0("k = ", best_k_3up, " (", sprintf("%.3f", best_sil),
                         ")")),
  tibble(group  = "Linkage method (sizes at k = 6)",
         check  = names(linkage_sizes),
         result = map_chr(linkage_sizes, \(x) paste(x, collapse = ", "))),
  tibble(group  = "Agreement (adjusted Rand index)",
         check  = c("Ward against k-means, all households",
                    paste0("Ward against Ward without the ", sum(!keep_hh),
                           " extreme households (n = ", sum(keep_hh), ")")),
         result = sprintf("%.3f", c(ari_kmeans, ari_trimmed))),
  tibble(group  = "Average silhouette width by segment",
         check  = sil_by_seg$segment,
         result = sprintf("%.3f", sil_by_seg$width))
)

robust_tbl |>
  gt(groupname_col = "group") |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", result = "Result")
```

```{r}
#| label: robust-values

# Look-ups for the paragraph below
complete_min <- min(linkage_sizes$Complete)
average_max  <- max(linkage_sizes$Average)
sil_weakest  <- slice_min(sil_by_seg, width)
sil_strongest <- slice_max(sil_by_seg, width)
```

@tbl-robust gives the results.

- **Six is the best number of groups once two is set aside.** From three to ten groups the average silhouette is highest at `r best_k_3up`.
- **Ward's linkage is the only one of the three that gives usable segments.** On the same distances, complete linkage leaves a group of only `r complete_min` household`r if (complete_min == 1) "" else "s"` and average linkage puts `r average_max` of the `r nrow(cluster_data)` households in one group. Neither could be turned into six campaigns.
- **Agreement with k-means is moderate.** The ARI is `r sprintf("%.3f", ari_kmeans)`, so k-means finds a similar structure but moves many households between neighbouring groups. This is a stricter and less flattering figure than the `r percent(agreement, accuracy = 0.1)` best-match share.
- **Most of the structure holds without the extreme households.** Removing the `r sum(!keep_hh)` households with a standardised value beyond 3 (@sec-prep) and clustering the other `r sum(keep_hh)` again gives an ARI of `r sprintf("%.3f", ari_trimmed)` with the original segments. Most of the structure survives, although some households change group.
- **Some segments are much sharper than others.** The average silhouette width runs from `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_strongest$width)` for the `r sil_strongest$segment` to `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_weakest$width)` for the `r sil_weakest$segment`. The first is a clearly separate group, while the second sits close to its neighbours, which matches its low k-means agreement above.

So the six segments have real cores, but their borders are not sharp, and the weakest segments should be read as tendencies rather than fixed types.

## Describing each group (2d)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-segment-means
#| tbl-cap: "How each segment buys bath soap, in original units, with the all-household average in the last row."

# Attach each household's segment to its original (untransformed) values
original_segment <- soap_clusters |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars)),
            by = "MemberID")

# Group sizes and means, plus an all-households row for comparison
segment_means <- original_segment |>
  group_by(cluster, segment) |>
  summarise(households = n(), across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  bind_rows(original_segment |>
              summarise(households = n(), across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean)) |>
              mutate(segment = "All households"))

segment_means |>
  select(-cluster) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(TotalVol, NoTrans, NoBrands), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(c(PurPromo6, PurOtherPromo, MaxBrShare), decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             TotalVol = "Total volume", NoTrans = "Transactions",
             PurPromo6 = "Share on promo 6",
             PurOtherPromo = "Share on other promos",
             NoBrands = "Brands bought", MaxBrShare = "Share to top brand") |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(rows = segment == "All households"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-centroids
#| fig-cap: "Segment centroids: the mean of each standardised variable within each segment (0 = the average household)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

soap_prep |>
  left_join(soap_clusters, by = "MemberID") |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean)) |>
  pivot_longer(-segment, names_to = "variable", values_to = "mean_z") |>
  mutate(segment  = factor(segment, levels = segment_names),
         variable = factor(variable, levels = rev(cluster_vars))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_z, variable, fill = mean_z > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~segment, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[4])) +
  labs(title = "Segment centroids on the six purchase variables",
       x = "Standardised mean (0 = average household)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: segment-values

# Look-ups for the paragraphs below, so every number comes from the table above
seg_mean <- \(seg, col) segment_means[[col]][segment_means$segment == seg]
all_mean <- \(col) seg_mean("All households", col)
seg_size <- \(seg) seg_mean(seg, "households")
fmt_pct  <- \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 1)
fmt_vol  <- \(x) comma(x, accuracy = 100)
n_hh     <- nrow(soap_prep)

# BrOthers was not clustered on, so it is only used to profile the segments
brothers_seg <- soap_clusters |>
  left_join(select(soap, MemberID, BrOthers, MaxBrShare), by = "MemberID") |>
  summarise(brothers = mean(BrOthers), zero_max = sum(near(MaxBrShare, 0)),
            .by = segment)
brothers_of <- \(seg) brothers_seg$brothers[brothers_seg$segment == seg]
zero_of     <- \(seg) brothers_seg$zero_max[brothers_seg$segment == seg]
zero_segs   <- brothers_seg |> filter(zero_max > 0) |> arrange(desc(zero_max))
```

@tbl-segment-means gives each segment's size and average purchase behaviour in original units, with the average for all households in the last row. @fig-centroids shows the same segments on the standardised scale: bars to the right are above the average household and bars to the left are below it, so the longest bars show what makes each segment distinctive.

**Small-brand regular-price buyers** (`r seg_size("Small-brand regular-price buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Small-brand regular-price buyers") / n_hh)` of the panel). These households buy close to the average amount of soap, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "TotalVol"))` units over `r round(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "NoTrans"))` transactions, and rarely buy on promotion (`r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "PurPromo6"))` of volume on promotion 6 and `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` on other promotions). Only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of their volume goes to their top named brand, well below the average of `r fmt_pct(all_mean("MaxBrShare"))`, so the eight named brands win little of their spending. Instead, `r fmt_pct(brothers_of("Small-brand regular-price buyers"))` of their volume goes to `BrOthers`, the brands outside the eight named, the highest of any segment. `BrOthers` was not a clustering variable, so this is a profiling observation. It is not evidence of loyalty either, because `BrOthers` pools many small brands and cannot show whether a household stays with one of them. Because they rarely buy on promotion, discounts are unlikely to change their habits.

**Heavy multi-brand shoppers** (`r seg_size("Heavy multi-brand shoppers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Heavy multi-brand shoppers") / n_hh)`). This segment buys the most soap, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "TotalVol"))` units, which is `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "TotalVol") / all_mean("TotalVol") - 1)` more than the average household, and buys most often, with about `r round(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "NoTrans"))` transactions against an average of `r round(all_mean("NoTrans"))`. They spread their volume over the most brands (`r round(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "NoBrands"), 1)` on average against `r round(all_mean("NoBrands"), 1)` overall) with only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "MaxBrShare"))` going to their top brand. Their volume is large but divided between brands, so reward schemes that encourage them to keep buying the same brand suit this segment.

**Light occasional buyers** (`r seg_size("Light occasional buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Light occasional buyers") / n_hh)`). These households buy very little, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "TotalVol"))` units over only `r round(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "NoTrans"), 1)` transactions, only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "TotalVol") / all_mean("TotalVol"))` of the average volume. They did not buy on promotion at all and bought the fewest brands (`r round(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` against `r round(all_mean("NoBrands"), 1)`). Given their small volume they should be a low priority for promotion spending.

**Loyal regular-price buyers** (`r seg_size("Loyal regular-price buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Loyal regular-price buyers") / n_hh)`). These households buy slightly more than average, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, in fewer transactions (`r round(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "NoTrans"))` against `r round(all_mean("NoTrans"))`). They give `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of their volume to one brand and almost never buy on promotion (`r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PurPromo6"))` on promotion 6 and `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` on others). Since they already buy their favourite brand without discounts, reward schemes that maintain their loyalty suit them better than price promotions, which would only give away margin.

**Loyal promotion buyers** (`r seg_size("Loyal promotion buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Loyal promotion buyers") / n_hh)`). This is the most loyal segment, with `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of volume going to one brand and only `r round(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` brands bought on average. They buy an average amount, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, but `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` of their volume is bought on other promotions, about `r round(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "PurOtherPromo") / all_mean("PurOtherPromo"), 1)` times the average of `r fmt_pct(all_mean("PurOtherPromo"))`. Because this segment is loyal and also responds to promotions, promotions on their favourite brand suit them.

**Promo-6 buyers** (`r seg_size("Promo-6 buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Promo-6 buyers") / n_hh)`). These households buy slightly less than average, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, at an average frequency. They are among the least loyal, with only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of volume going to their top brand across `r round(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` brands, and `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "PurPromo6"))` of their volume is bought on promotion 6, about `r round(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "PurPromo6") / all_mean("PurPromo6"), 1)` times the average of `r fmt_pct(all_mean("PurPromo6"))`. Their low `MaxBrShare` is partly a small-brand effect too, since `r fmt_pct(brothers_of("Promo-6 buyers"))` of their volume goes to `BrOthers`. Promotion 6 offers timed at different points of the year suit this segment best.

**Where the `MaxBrShare` = 0 households went.** Question 1 showed that the `r nrow(zero_hh)` households with `MaxBrShare` = 0 buy only one brand, which sits inside `BrOthers`. They are not spread evenly: `r paste0(zero_segs$zero_max, if_else(zero_segs$zero_max == 1, " is", " are"), " in the ", zero_segs$segment, collapse = ", ")`. On `MaxBrShare` they look like the least loyal households, so the clustering places most of them in low-concentration segments even though each one is fully loyal to a small brand. This is the limit that Question 1 item 7 warned about, and it is one more reason the low `MaxBrShare` of the Small-brand regular-price and Promo-6 buyers should not be read as plain disloyalty.


# Question 2(e): Profiling the Groups {#sec-profile}

The segments in @sec-cluster were built from purchase behaviour only. Demographics were deliberately left out of the clustering, so that the groups describe *how* households buy rather than *who* they are. This section brings the demographics back to answer the client's next question: who are the households in each segment, and how can they be reached?

## Which three demographics, and why

Each variable was chosen because a difference between segments on it leads to a different business action (@tbl-profile-vars).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-vars
#| tbl-cap: "The three profiling demographics and the business lever each one informs."

# The three demographics used to profile the segments
profile_vars <- c("SEC", "HS", "AGE")

# Missing values per profile variable (zeros were turned into NA in Section 7)
profile_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(all_of(profile_vars), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

tibble(
  variable = profile_vars,
  type     = c("Ordinal, 1 high to 4 low", "Numeric, number of members",
               "Ordinal, 1 young to 4 old"),
  action   = c("Price point and value or premium range",
               "Pack size and multi-packs",
               "Media channel and message")
) |>
  left_join(profile_missing, by = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", type = "Type",
             action = "Business lever it informs",
             n_missing = "Missing households")
```

```{r}
#| label: other-demographics

other_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(c(FEH, MT, SEX, EDU, CHILD, CS, Affluence),
                   \(x) sum(is.na(x))))
share_female <- mean(soap_clean$SEX == 2, na.rm = TRUE)
# Spearman correlation, because SEC is ordinal
sec_aff_cor  <- cor(soap_clean$SEC, soap_clean$Affluence, method = "spearman",
                    use = "complete.obs")
```

- **SEC (socioeconomic class)** tells a manufacturer what price a segment can bear. SEC is also one of the strata the panel was sampled on, so all `r nrow(soap_clean) - profile_missing$n_missing[profile_missing$variable == "SEC"]` households have a value and each class holds exactly a quarter of the panel, which makes any tilt within a segment easy to read.
- **HS (household size)** is the demographic most directly tied to how much soap a household uses, so it tells the client which segments suit larger packs or multi-packs. `r profile_missing$n_missing[profile_missing$variable == "HS"]` households have no size recorded and are left out of the HS summaries only.
- **AGE (age of the homemaker)** tells an advertising agency where and how to speak to each segment. Every household has a value.

**Why not the others.** `Affluence` overlaps with SEC (Spearman correlation `r round(sec_aff_cor, 2)`; SEC runs from 1 high to 4 low, so a negative value means wealthier households sit in the higher classes) and has `r other_missing$Affluence` missing households. `MT` (native language) and `CHILD` are codes with no labels in the data guide, so a difference could not be turned into an action. `SEX` barely varies: `r percent(share_female, accuracy = 1)` of homemakers with a recorded value are female. `EDU`, `FEH` and `CS` are missing for `r other_missing$EDU`, `r other_missing$FEH` and `r other_missing$CS` households and are less directly linked to a bath soap decision. @sec-profile-check tests this choice against the data.

**Missing values.** No household is dropped from the segmentation. For HS, each summary and test uses only the households that have a value, and the number used is shown.

## Profile by group

```{r}
#| label: profile-data

# Attach the three demographics (and TotalVol, to link size to volume) to each
# household's segment
profile_df <- soap_clusters |>
  select(MemberID, cluster, segment) |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(profile_vars), TotalVol),
            by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(
    # Readable labels for the ordinal codes
    SEC = factor(SEC, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 High", "2", "3", "4 Low")),
    AGE = factor(AGE, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 Young", "2", "3", "4 Old")),
    segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_names)
  )

# One chart function for both categorical variables, so they look the same
plot_props <- function(data, var, title) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ var }})) |>
    count(segment, {{ var }}) |>
    group_by(segment) |>
    mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>                 # share within each segment
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(prop, fct_rev(segment), fill = {{ var }})) +
    geom_col(colour = "white") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
    labs(title = title, y = NULL, x = "Share of households in the segment",
         fill = NULL)
}

# Per-segment summary used in the text and in the summary table
seg_profile <- profile_df |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(households = n(),
            sec_high  = mean(as.integer(SEC) <= 2),     # SEC 1 or 2
            sec_low   = mean(as.integer(SEC) == 4),     # SEC 4
            hs_n      = sum(!is.na(HS)),
            hs_mean   = mean(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            hs_median = median(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            age_old   = mean(AGE == "4 Old"),
            volume    = mean(TotalVol))
```

```{r}
#| label: profile-tests-compute

# Cramer's V (Cramer, 1946): chi-squared rescaled to run from 0 to 1
cramers_v <- function(tab, stat) sqrt(stat / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1)))

# Chi-squared test plus Cramer's V for one categorical variable
chisq_row <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(d$segment, d[[var]])
  # simulated p-value, see below
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 5000)
  tibble(variable = var, test = "Chi-squared", n = sum(tab),
         p_value = res$p.value,
         effect = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         effect_measure = "Cramer's V")
}

# only households with a recorded size
hs_df <- profile_df |> filter(!is.na(HS))

set.seed(55789)   # the simulated p-values are random, so fix them
kw_hs <- kruskal.test(HS ~ segment, data = hs_df)

profile_tests <- bind_rows(
  chisq_row(profile_df, "SEC"),
  tibble(variable = "HS", test = "Kruskal-Wallis", n = nrow(hs_df),
         p_value = kw_hs$p.value,
         # epsilon squared
         effect = unname(kw_hs$statistic) / (nrow(hs_df) - 1),
         effect_measure = "Epsilon squared"),
  chisq_row(profile_df, "AGE")
)

# Small helpers for the text
seg_prof <- \(seg, col) seg_profile[[col]][seg_profile$segment == seg]
fmt_p    <- \(p) if_else(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste("p =", sprintf("%.3f",
                                                                      p)))
test_row <- \(var) profile_tests |> filter(variable == var)
```

### Socioeconomic class

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-sec
#| fig-cap: "Socioeconomic class within each segment (1 = highest, 4 = lowest). Across the panel each class holds 25% of households."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

plot_props(profile_df, SEC, "Socioeconomic class within each segment")
```

@fig-profile-sec shows the class mix. Because the panel is stratified on SEC, every class holds 25% of households overall, so a segment that departs from a quarter in a class genuinely leans that way. The **Loyal promotion buyers** have the most lower-class households: `r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Loyal promotion buyers", "sec_low"))` are in SEC 4. Together with their high use of other promotions (@sec-cluster), this points to a budget-conscious group that stays with one brand but buys more of it when it is on offer, so price promotions *on their favourite brand* reach them well. The **Promo-6 buyers** lean the other way, with `r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Promo-6 buyers", "sec_high"))` in SEC 1 or 2 against `r fmt_pct(mean(as.integer(profile_df$SEC) <= 2))` overall: their heavy use of promotion 6 looks like a deal-seeking habit rather than a sign that they cannot afford full price, so the *timing* of promotion 6 matters more than a cheaper product. The test confirms a real but small difference (`r fmt_p(test_row("SEC")$p_value)`, Cram<U+00E9>r's V = `r round(test_row("SEC")$effect, 3)`), so SEC is a useful secondary guide, not a targeting rule on its own.

### Household size

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-hs
#| fig-cap: "Household size within each segment (households with a recorded size only). The cross marks the mean."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

hs_df |>
  ggplot(aes(HS, fct_rev(segment), fill = segment)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 4, size = 3,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(title = "Household size within each segment",
       subtitle = paste0("Households with a recorded size: n = ", nrow(hs_df)),
       y = NULL, x = "Members in the household")
```

@fig-profile-hs shows household size. The **Heavy multi-brand shoppers** have the largest households (`r round(seg_prof("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "hs_mean"), 1)` members on average against `r round(mean(hs_df$HS), 1)` overall) and also buy the most soap, which fits the simple logic that more people use more soap. For a client this is the natural segment for family packs and multi-packs, ideally tied to one brand to counter their habit of spreading volume across brands. The **Small-brand regular-price buyers** and **Promo-6 buyers** have the smallest households (`r round(seg_prof("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "hs_mean"), 1)` and `r round(seg_prof("Promo-6 buyers", "hs_mean"), 1)` members), so standard packs suit them. The difference is statistically significant but small (`r fmt_p(test_row("HS")$p_value)`, epsilon squared = `r round(test_row("HS")$effect, 3)`).

One pattern needs a warning: only `r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "hs_n")` of the `r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households")` **Light occasional buyers** have a recorded household size. The largest share of the `r sum(is.na(soap_clean$HS))` households with no household size (which also lack education, language, gender, TV and Affluence, @sec-prep) falls into this segment (`r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households") - seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "hs_n")` of them), so it may partly reflect households with incomplete panel records rather than a true customer type, so its household size profile should not be relied on. Its `SEC` and `AGE` are recorded for every household, so those two comparisons still hold.

### Age of the homemaker

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-age
#| fig-cap: "Age of the homemaker within each segment (1 = youngest, 4 = oldest)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

plot_props(profile_df, AGE, "Age of the homemaker within each segment")
```

@fig-profile-age shows that age does **not** separate the segments (`r fmt_p(test_row("AGE")$p_value)`, Cram<U+00E9>r's V = `r round(test_row("AGE")$effect, 3)`). Older homemakers are the largest group in every segment, from `r fmt_pct(min(seg_profile$age_old))` to `r fmt_pct(max(seg_profile$age_old))` in the oldest class, and the differences in the chart are within what chance would produce. The practical conclusion is that age gives no reason to reach one segment through a different media channel from another.

## Are the differences real?

A chart can show a difference that is only noise, so each variable is tested. SEC and AGE are categorical, so a **chi-squared test of independence** checks whether the mix of classes differs between segments. Some cells are small (few households have the youngest age code), so the p-value is simulated rather than taken from the chi-squared table, which keeps it valid when expected counts are below 5. HS is a count with a long right tail, so the **Kruskal-Wallis test**, which compares segments on ranks rather than means, is used instead of ANOVA. With `r nrow(profile_df)` households even a tiny difference can be "significant", so an effect size is also reported: Cram<U+00E9>r's V [@cramer1946] for the categorical variables and epsilon squared for HS, both running from 0 (no association) to 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Do the segments differ on each demographic?"

profile_tests |>
  select(variable, test, n, p_value, effect, effect_measure) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(effect, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(p_value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", test = "Test", n = "Households used",
             p_value = "p-value", effect = "Effect size",
             effect_measure = "Measure")
```

@tbl-profile-tests gives the results. SEC and household size differ significantly between segments, but both effects are small, and age does not differ at all. **The segments are therefore only weakly visible in demographics.** That is a finding in itself, and it supports XYZ's move to behavioural segmentation: a client could not have found these segments from demographics alone, so targeting should run on purchase data (panel or loyalty card records), with SEC and household size used to fine-tune the offer.

The next two sections go beyond the question. They show which segments and classes cause the differences, and test whether a better demographic was left out.

## Extra check: where do the differences come from?

The tests above say *whether* the segments differ. This check says *which* segment and class cause it, so a client knows where to act. For SEC and AGE, the **standardised residual** of each cell compares the number of households in that segment and class with the number expected if every segment had the same mix. A value beyond <U+00B1>2 marks a clear excess (positive) or shortfall (negative). For HS, **pairwise Wilcoxon tests** compare every pair of segments, with the **Holm adjustment** keeping the overall chance of a false difference at 5% across all the comparisons.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Standardised residuals of segment by SEC and by AGE. Beyond plus or minus 2 is a clear difference."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Standardised residuals of the segment by class table, in long form for
# plotting
resid_df <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(segment = d$segment, level = d[[var]])
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning. Only the residuals are used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  as.data.frame.table(res$stdres, responseName = "resid") |>
    mutate(variable = var)
}

plot_resid <- function(rd, title) {
  ggplot(rd, aes(level, fct_rev(segment), fill = resid)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(resid, 1), colour = abs(resid) > 2),
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal_ink, `FALSE` = pal_ink)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal_lo, mid = "white", high = pal_hi,
                         midpoint = 0) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Residual")
}

sec_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "SEC")
age_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "AGE")

plot_resid(sec_resid, "Socioeconomic class") +
  plot_resid(age_resid, "Age of the homemaker")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-hs-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "Household size: segment pairs that still differ after the Holm adjustment."

hs_pairs <- pairwise.wilcox.test(hs_df$HS, hs_df$segment,
                                 p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE) |>
  tidy()

hs_pairs |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(p.value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(group1 = "Segment", group2 = "Compared with",
             p.value = "Holm-adjusted p-value")
```

```{r}
#| label: residual-values

resid_text <- \(seg, lvl) {
  sprintf("%+.1f",
          sec_resid$resid[sec_resid$segment == seg & sec_resid$level == lvl])
}
n_age_cells <- sum(abs(age_resid$resid) > 2)
```

@fig-profile-residuals and @tbl-profile-hs-pairs show the detail. The SEC result is driven by three segments: the Loyal promotion buyers have more SEC 4 households than expected (`r resid_text("Loyal promotion buyers", "4 Low")`), the Promo-6 buyers have more SEC 2 households (`r resid_text("Promo-6 buyers", "2")`), and the small Light occasional group has more SEC 1 households (`r resid_text("Light occasional buyers", "1 High")`). `r if (n_age_cells == 0) "No age cell goes beyond 2 in either direction, which matches the non-significant age test." else paste(n_age_cells, "age cells go beyond 2 in either direction, but the age test as a whole is not significant.")` For household size, only the pairs in the table above differ after adjustment, and every one of them involves the Heavy multi-brand shoppers' larger households. These are the comparisons a client should rely on when choosing which segment gets which offer.

## Extra check: did we miss a better demographic? {#sec-profile-check}

The three variables were chosen for business reasons. As a check, every demographic is measured on how strongly it separates the segments with one common measure, Cram<U+00E9>r's V. Numeric variables (HS, Affluence and EDU, which has nine sparse levels) are first cut into four equal-sized groups, and native-language codes held by fewer than 20 households are pooled, so that rare codes do not inflate the measure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-all-demographics
#| fig-cap: "How strongly each demographic separates the six segments (Cramer's V)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

all_demo_v <- map_dfr(demo_cols, \(v) {
  d <- soap_clusters |>
    select(MemberID, segment) |>
    left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, value = all_of(v)),
              by = "MemberID") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))
  grp <- if (v %in% c("HS", "Affluence", "EDU")) {
    # numeric: four equal-sized groups
    factor(ntile(d$value, 4))
  } else {
    # categorical: pool rare codes
    fct_lump_min(factor(d$value), min = 20)
  }
  tab <- table(d$segment, grp)
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning. Only the statistic is used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  tibble(variable = v, n = nrow(d),
         cramers_v = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         chosen = v %in% profile_vars)
})

all_demo_v |>
  ggplot(aes(cramers_v, fct_reorder(variable, cramers_v), fill = chosen)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Chosen", `FALSE` = "Not chosen")) +
  labs(title = "How strongly each demographic separates the segments",
       x = "Cramer's V", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-values

demo_v <- \(v) round(all_demo_v$cramers_v[all_demo_v$variable == v], 3)
```

@fig-profile-all-demographics shows that every demographic separates the segments only weakly (the largest V is `r round(max(all_demo_v$cramers_v), 3)`), which repeats the finding above. HS and SEC are among the stronger variables, which supports two of the three choices. `Affluence` (V = `r demo_v("Affluence")`) and `EDU` (`r demo_v("EDU")`) separate the segments more than AGE (`r demo_v("AGE")`). They were left out because Affluence largely repeats SEC and EDU has many sparse levels and more missing values. Since the brief lets the team choose any three demographics, Affluence would be an acceptable alternative to AGE. It is reported here so a reader can see the trade-off rather than take the choice on trust.


## Summary profile of each segment

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Demographic profile of each segment."

seg_profile |>
  select(segment, households, sec_high, sec_low, hs_median, hs_mean, age_old) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(c(sec_high, sec_low, age_old), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(hs_mean, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             sec_high = "SEC 1 or 2", sec_low = "SEC 4",
             hs_median = "Median size", hs_mean = "Mean size",
             age_old = "Homemaker AGE 4") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Socioeconomic class", columns = c(sec_high, sec_low)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Household size", columns = c(hs_median, hs_mean))
```

@tbl-profile-summary brings the profile together. Putting purchase behaviour (@sec-cluster) and demographics together:

- **Heavy multi-brand shoppers:** the largest households and the most volume. Family packs and multi-packs, combined with a reward scheme that concentrates their spending on one brand.
- **Loyal promotion buyers:** the most lower-class households (`r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Loyal promotion buyers", "sec_low"))` in SEC 4). Value packs and price promotions on the brand they already favour.
- **Promo-6 buyers:** more higher-class households than average (`r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Promo-6 buyers", "sec_high"))` in SEC 1 or 2). Promotion 6 offers spread through the year; a cheaper product is not needed.
- **Loyal regular-price buyers:** demographically close to the average household. Reward schemes rather than discounts, which they do not need.
- **Small-brand regular-price buyers:** close to average with smaller households, so demographics give little extra help in finding them; they are best reached through purchase data, with trial and visibility to win them from small brands.
- **Light occasional buyers:** too small, too light and too poorly recorded (`r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households") - seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "hs_n")` of `r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households")` have no household size, education or TV record) to target separately.


# Question 3: Dimension Reduction with PCA {#sec-pca}

Question 2 described each household with six purchase behaviour variables. **Principal component analysis (PCA)** asks whether those six can be summarised by fewer new variables, called components, without losing much information. Each component is a weighted combination of the six: the first captures as much of the variation between households as possible, the second captures as much of what is left as possible while being uncorrelated with the first, and so on. If the six variables overlap, a few components carry most of the information, which makes the households easier to describe and to plot.

## Is PCA worth doing on these variables?

PCA can only compress variables that move together. If the six were unrelated, every component would carry about the same share and nothing would be gained.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-correlation
#| tbl-cap: "Correlations between the six prepared variables (the same data the clustering used)."

pca_cor <- soap_prep |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  cor()

# The strongest pair, and each variable's largest correlation with any other
top_pair <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(var1 < var2) |>                       # each pair once, no diagonal
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 1)

loner <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  pivot_longer(-variable, names_to = "other", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(variable != other) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(max_abs_r = max(abs(r))) |>
  slice_min(max_abs_r, n = 1)

as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(-variable, decimals = 2) |>
  data_color(columns = -variable,
             palette = c(pal_lo, "#F9E1EB", pal_hi),
             domain = c(-1, 1), autocolor_text = FALSE)
```

@tbl-pca-correlation shows the correlations. The strongest relationship is between `r top_pair$var1` and `r top_pair$var2` (r = `r round(top_pair$r, 2)`), so there is real overlap for PCA to use. At the other extreme, `r loner$variable` is almost independent of the rest (its largest correlation with any other variable is `r round(loner$max_abs_r, 2)`), so it cannot be folded into the others and is likely to need a component of its own.

## Running the PCA

The PCA follows the tidymodels recipe pattern [@kuhn2020tidymodels; @R-recipes]: a recipe with `step_normalize()` and `step_pca()`, estimated with `prep()`, and checked against base R's `prcomp()`.

```{r}
#| label: pca-fit

pca_data <- soap_prep |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars))

pca_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = pca_data) |>
  # keep the ID, but leave it out of the PCA
  update_role(MemberID, new_role = "id") |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>     # see the note below
  # keep all six for now
  step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = length(cluster_vars),
           id = "pca") |>
  prep()

# What step_normalize learned: for already standardised data, means are 0 and
# sds are 1
norm_check <- tidy(pca_rec, number = 1) |>
  group_by(statistic) |>
  summarise(furthest = max(abs(value - if_else(statistic == "mean", 0, 1))))

# Cross-check against base R: prcomp() should give the same variances
pca_base <- prcomp(select(pca_data, all_of(cluster_vars)))
```

**Is `step_normalize()` needed again?** PCA must be run on standardised data, otherwise the variable with the largest units (volume) would dominate the first component only because its numbers are bigger. `soap_prep` was already standardised in @sec-prep, so this step changes nothing here: the means it learned differ from 0, and the standard deviations from 1, by at most `r sprintf("%.0e", max(norm_check$furthest))`, which is rounding error. It is kept so that the recipe is safe on its own if it is ever run on unprepared data. All six components are kept at this stage so that the number to retain is chosen from the evidence below rather than fixed in advance.

## How many components to keep

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-variance
#| tbl-cap: "Variance explained by each component."

pca_var <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "variance") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  transmute(component,
            eigenvalue = variance,
            percent    = `percent variance`,
            cumulative = `cumulative percent variance`)

# The variances match base R's prcomp() (eigenvalue = sd squared)
same_as_prcomp <- isTRUE(all.equal(pca_var$eigenvalue, pca_base$sdev^2,
                                   check.attributes = FALSE))

pca_var |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(eigenvalue, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(c(percent, cumulative), decimals = 1, pattern = "{x}%") |>
  cols_label(component = "Component", eigenvalue = "Eigenvalue",
             percent = "Variance explained", cumulative = "Cumulative")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-scree
#| fig-cap: "Left: scree plot with the eigenvalue of 1 marked. Right: cumulative variance with the 70% line."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

# Kaiser: eigenvalue above 1
n_kaiser <- sum(pca_var$eigenvalue > 1)
# enough components for 70% of the variation
n_70     <- which(pca_var$cumulative >= 70)[1]
# the decision (explained below)
n_keep   <- n_70

scree <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, eigenvalue)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(colour = pal[1]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = component <= n_keep), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  labs(title = "Scree plot", x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue")

cumul <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, cumulative / 100)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = component <= n_keep), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative variance explained", x = "Component", y = NULL)

scree + cumul
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-keep-values
```
